The NBA Rookie of the Year race is beginning to take shape after the first month of the 2026-27 season, though no player has managed to separate himself from the pack. AJ Dybantsa and Darryn Peterson lurk closely behind after slower starts to the campaign, and there's a collection of other rookies contributing in significant ways with many teams emphasizing depth to combat the NBA's injury issues.

Here's how the top NBA rookies stack up after the first month of the 2026-27 regular season.

NBA POWER RANKINGS: Giannis, Heat surge; Warriors plunge without Curry

#2653. Jon Anik: Claims of Daniel Cormier bias as UFC commentator are 'just straight lunacy'

Lead UFC play-by-play announcer Jon Anik believes Daniel Cormier has received unfair criticism for his UFC 334 commentary.

Many fans on social media took umbrage with Cormier acknowledging Ciryl Gane's work when he was getting heavily pressured by Josh Hokit (10-1 MMA, 4-1 UFC) early. Gane (15-2 MMA, 12-2 UFC) wound up bing awarded three rounds in a unanimous decision win, but Cormier had him winning four.

People have gone as far as creating a petition to remove Cormier as a UFC commentator, which has garnered over 8,000 signatures.

"I understand a lot of people are coming at Daniel Cormier, and I would agree in some part that maybe he was too insistent on the broadcast that Ciryl Gane had won Rounds 1 and 2," Anik said on his "Anik & Florian Podcast." "I guess my issue is just that there's just sort of a lot of venom, and I guess sort of anger out there when it comes to the fight and how it was scored. Dana White had it 4-1 Ciryl Gane. Kenny Florian had it same way Dana White did. There are other people who are supremely high-level fighters who had the fight for Josh Hokit."

Cormier insists he has zero beef with Hokit and revealed they even spoke on the phone after the fight.

"In terms of any bias from Daniel Cormier, when I read things like, 'Oh, because of Josh Hokit's wayward, terrible line about Michelle Obama,' and it was one of the worst utterances I've ever heard, but because of that line, somehow DC is going to be on the Ciryl Gane side or his scorecard would go that way," Anik said.

"I mean, it's just straight lunacy, and I can't help but defend my broadcast partner, you know? It's not like DC and I are best friends. We have friction like a married couple, but, man, does it make me want to come to his defense when I see some of the stuff that is out there just because there's just no bias."

#2652. Connor Hellebuyck trade: Jets send star goalie to the Devils in exchange for four players, two draft picks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Connor Hellebuyck is a now a Devil. The star goalie for the Winnipeg Jets is on the move after being traded to New Jersey on Friday in exchange for four players and two future draft picks. the teams announced the move with the Jets receiving Dawson Mercer, Nick Bjugstad, Nico Daws and Alexander Command, plus a 2027 seventh-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick.

Hellebuyck expressed his desire to be traded in the offseason when he formally requested a move in August. He said at the time that he had made the request months earlier and tried to keep the situation private.

Hellebuyck has spent his entire career with Winnipeg after being drafted by the Jets in 2012 at No. 130 overall. He's recognized as one of the best goalies in the league as a three-time Vezina Trophy winner. He also helped carry the United States to its first gold medal since 1980 at the 2026 Olympics in February with some incredible saves against Canada in the final game.

After trading Jacob Markstom in the offseason, the Devils had a clear need in goal, and this splashy move certainly fills that need. With a talented young core already in place, New Jersey's Stanley Cup window is wide open.

RAISE HELLE!Connor Hellebuyck is a New Jersey Devil: https://t.co/HCehRGOQI5 pic.twitter.com/dZGNQR16m1

For the Jets, it must be a hard pill to swallow when a franchise icon decides to walk out they door, but this trade package should help them as the enter a new era and revamp the roster. Winnipeg got a former first-rounder in Mercer to try and add to a rebuild as well as a veteran presence in Bjugstad. They also acquired a younger goalie in Daws who could fill the role of Hellebuyck at just 25 years old.

Goaltending has been an issue in New Jersey for a while now -- even after the team acquired Markstrom from the Calgary Flames in 2024. Markstom never really panned out, and his 13.6 goals allowed above average, per Natural Stat Trick, were a big reason why the Devils missed the postseason last year.

In the early portion of this season, it was clear that New Jersey needed to make a move to upgrade in the crease. Daws and veteran Jake Allen simply aren't a tandem suitable for a Stanley Cup contender, and the numbers backed that up. New Jersey ranks 24th in team save percentage at .877, and the duo of Daws and Allen combined to surrender 2.99 goals above average.

Once Hellebuyck gets up to game speed, that shouldn't be a problem anymore.

In the three-season stretch from 2023-26, Hellebuyck led the NHL with 73.42 goals saved above average, which is 20 goals higher than the next closest netminder. Over that span, Hellebuyck also posted a standard save percentage of .914 and an astronomical high-danger save-percentage of .832.

Hellebuyck carried less talented teams to the playoffs multiple times in his career. Now on a team loaded with weaponry in their prime -- Jack Hughes, Jesper Bratt and Nico Hischier to name a few -- Hellebuyck could be the final piece to the championship puzzle.

In terms of the acquisition cost, it was probably an easy deal for Devils general manager Sunny Mehta to make. The 2029 second-round pick is useless for a team that should be all-in now, Bjugstad is simply a depth piece and Daws now has no path to a starting role with Hellebuyck in town.

The most interesting trade chips are Mercer and Command. Mercer flashed major upside with 56 points in his second NHL season, 2022-23, but he hasn't really come close to hitting those heights again. Still, even if he has plateaued, Mercer remains a strong middle-six forward rising into his prime.

Although Command had his detractors -- and may have been over-drafted at No. 12 overall -- he was a consensus first-round pick last summer. That gives Winnipeg a potential franchise forward it can build around long-term, but New Jersey already has one of the deepest forward groups in the league, especially with the emergence of Arseny Gritsyuk and the acquisition of Luke Evangelista.

If we're looking for a 3-D chess angle of this deal, it only makes the Devils more appealing for a certain Minnesota Wild defenseman whose brothers just happen to play in New Jersey already. Grade -- A+

Let's get the obvious out of the way first: The Jets were never going to get fair value for Hellebuyck because, at his best, he's the No. 1 goaltender in the world with no equal. That type of excellence can't be replaced.

That said, Winnipeg did fairly well given the circumstances. Hellebuyck made a public trade request, and he wasn't even with the team after sitting out for the entirety of training camp. The entire league knew the Jets had to trade him.

Hellebuyck's talent created a decent market anyway, but most of the suitors were bona fide Stanley Cup contenders with little in the way of valuable draft capital, and they weren't going to knee cap the roster by sending a key player back in return.

With all that taken into consideration, Kevin Cheveldayoff got a solid return. Although Mercer's ceiling may be lower than initially thought, he's a 24-year-old forward who banks roughly 20 goals and 20 assists every season. The kicker with Mercer will be Winnipeg's ability to re-sign him before he hits restricted free agency next summer.

The addition of Command means Winnipeg now has two forwards selected in the top 12 of the 2026 NHL Draft after taking center Viggo Bjorck themselves. If both of those players deliver on their first-round pedigrees, they could be a terrific one-two punch for the team long-term.

Daws was a third-round pick in 2020, and despite playing just 13 NHL games since the start of the 2024-25 season, he should give Winnipeg a solid back up option behind Stuart Skinner. It certainly helps that Skinner is off to a great start with his new team -- and if Daws develops into a true No. 1 -- it'll be gravy.

If there's any reason to critique this deal from the Jets' side of things, it's that they didn't get premium draft capital or a surefire up-and-coming prospect. Maybe Command develops into a star, but there's no guarantee he becomes a top-six stud in the NHL.

The Jets got a lot of good stuff, but they didn't really get anything great, at least not based on what we know in the moment. Because of that, I have to ding Winnipeg a little bit. Grade: B

#2651. Lakers coach has savage reaction to embarrassing loss to lowly Jazz

JJ Redick entered the Lakers' locker room on Wednesday night following the team's 109-97 loss to the Jazz at Crypto.com Arena with a simple question.

Who on the team felt like they played well in the Lakers' first loss in nearly three weeks?

There was no sugarcoating Wednesday's loss.

"We didn't play well," Redick said. "Nobody played well. It's not Walker, it's not Luka, it's not Q, it's not Sandro [Mamukelashvili]. Nobody had a great game."

Los Angeles Lakers head coach JJ Redick reacts during a game against the Utah Jazz at Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. Getty Images

Luka Doncic #77 of the Los Angeles Lakers attempts a shot against Mo Bamba #44 of the Utah Jazz. Getty Images

A quick look at the box score explains why.

Yes, Luka Dončić had 29 points, seven assists and five rebounds, but fatigue appeared to catch up to him – evident by his nine turnovers, 10-for-28 shooting from the field and his streak of scoring at least 30 points ending.

Yes, Quentin Grimes followed up his 47-point masterpiece during the win over the Hornets with a 20-point showing against the Jazz, but he scored two points and shot just 1 for 6 from the field during a fourth quarter the Lakers were outscored 31-21 on Wednesday.

Yes, Walker Kessler extended his double-double streak to six games, but he was the first to admit his scoring touch wasn't present (he shot 4 for 10 on free throws).

Ace Bailey of the Utah Jazz drives to the basket during a game against the Los Angeles Lakers. NBAE via Getty Images

The Lakers weren't overreacting to their nine-game winning streak game ending to a Jazz toward the bottom of the Western Conference standings.

The Lakers recognize that there are going to be games where it won't be their night in an 82-game season

Wednesday was one of those nights, with their shooting from all over the court falling well below the standard they've established for themselves.

Luka Doncic of the Los Angeles Lakers passes in front of Josh Green, Mo Bamba and Svi Mykhailiuk of the Utah Jazz. Getty Images

"You can't overemphasize a loss because we're still in a good spot," Jake LaRavia said. "We're going to stay connected as a team. We're not going to let this loss get to our heads too much. We got another opportunity Friday to bounce back."

Kessler added: "With 82 games, when you have a bad game like this, you don't want to spend too much time lingering on the losses. You want to learn from it and move on because you have to. Our offense, we were getting good looks. Just wasn't falling necessarily. So I don't think there's cause for concern."

#2646. Dr. J, Julius Randle rip into Nets after embarrassing loss to Bulls

This was a night the Brooklyn Nets could feel good and get a win. It was a night honoring the 1974 and 1976 ABA championship teams, and the struggling Chicago Bulls were in town, a game the Nets could, and maybe should, win.

Instead, the Nets got their doors blown off early and went on to lose by 30, 137-107.

The Nets broadcast brought on Julius Irving, the legendary Dr. J and greatest player in franchise history — the star of those championship teams — and he was the first to rip the team and the way the day was handled.

"We didn't really talk to the players," Irving said on the YES Network broadcast. "You know, their coach was doing all the talking, and they were getting their preparation in, doing their drills, and so on and so forth. And I fully anticipated the Nets to be so fired up in having us here that they would blow Chicago out, but I'm looking at 62-39. So I was wrong."

After the game, Julius Randle, one of the players brought in to lift the floor of this team, was much harsher, via Brian Lewis at the New York Post.

"That was embarrassing. Been in the league for 13 years, and that's one of the worst games I've ever been a part of. And not because of the score... but it's how we did it. That wasn't cool. Nothing about it was cool," Julius Randle said. "We've got to find a way to figure out the root of it or whatever, but that's just unacceptable...

"It's just a pride, an effort, the competitive spirit, all of that, it was nonexistent."

"Very disappointed, and it was just starting with effort. We were not a competitive group, we were not a connected group, we were not a selfless group," Nets coach Jordi Fernández said. "So, I saw selfishness, I saw pointing fingers, and I saw guys that didn't always play hard."

The Nets are 3-11 in a season where they don't even control their own first-round pick (Houston has swap rights). The team is rebuilding and wasn't expected to be fighting for a playoff spot, but with Randle and Michael Porter Jr. on the roster, the expectations were higher than this.

#2645. Why Man United staff feel treatment of Michael Carrick was 'disgusting' and the comment from Omar Berrada that raised eyebrows as club legend is put out of his misery - and Mauricio Pochettino gets set to take over

By CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER and DANIEL MATTHEWS, US SENIOR SPORTS WRITER

Published: 14:25 EST, 12 November 2026 | Updated: 07:15 EST, 13 November 2026

Mauricio Pochettino would have been fast asleep in his hotel room in the quirky American town of Trilith when Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox sat down with Michael Carrick at Carrington Thursday morning and confirmed the worst-kept secret in football.

It was time for Carrick to vacate the head coach’s office at Manchester United, and safe to say Pochettino will have his feet under the desk this time next week.

Carrick arrived at 7.50am but, unlike the last two days, he was no longer wearing his United training gear.

The agonising wait to be put out of his misery was over, and the club’s chief executive and director of football duly administered the last rites before Carrick left at 10.18am.

The decision was communicated to staff and Under-21s boss Adam Lawrence took training with the players who have remained at Carrington during the international break.

The first reports of Carrick’s sacking broke at 9.30am, but United insisted that they were premature and it wasn’t until 10.37am that the news was confirmed in a 142-word statement.

Michael Carrick finally left Carrington on Thursday morning after an agonising wait to be put out of his misery

Staff at Manchester United believe that the former club captain's treatment at the hands of their Ineos paymasters has been 'disgusting'

It's understood that his backroom staff - assistant Steve Holland, coaches Jonathan Woodgate, Jonny Evans and Travis Binnion, and goalkeeper coach Craig Mawson - have also gone. When Evans left on Wednesday night with his car piled high with cardboard boxes, it didn't bode well.

The treatment of Carrick and Evans, in particular, has upset staff. Two highly-respected figures at United, whose association with the club goes back more than 20 years, have been left hanging while their employers stumble over a succession plan.

Members of staff share Gary Neville’s view that Berrada and Wilcox meeting with Sir Jim Ratcliffe in Monaco, and making a move for Pochettino while Carrick had to keep driving past the cameras on his way into Carrington for the last three days, was ‘disgusting’.

It has also reignited anger over the 450 job cuts carried out by Ratcliffe and Ineos over the past three years while pouring millions down the drain in compensation.

The £10million to buy Pochettino and his staff out of their contracts with the US Soccer Federation, and the pay-off owing to Carrick and Co, will push the cost of hiring and firing coaches in the Ineos era close to £50m.

No wonder eyebrows were raised when Berrada spoke at Sir Alex Ferguson’s 40th anniversary dinner at Old Trafford on Friday night and talked about building a culture at the club.

The feeling is that changing United’s head coach won’t make a shred of difference if there isn’t significant change higher up the chain.

It has once again turned the spotlight on the relationship between Ratcliffe and the Glazer family, who from February can force him to sell his 28 per cent holding to a third party for less than the £25-per-share he paid in 2024 unless he can match the offer and buy the club himself.

However, United sources say they had little choice but to sack Carrick with the club in the relegation zone, having decided to give him a stay of execution at the end of last month.

Since then, the club had carried out a comprehensive review and come to the conclusion that a record of one win from 10 Premier League games was unacceptable.

The sources indicated that the United board shared the frustration and anger felt by fans over the situation, and believe that a change of head coach will bring about an improvement from a squad that is far better than results would suggest.

While United praised Carrick for his ‘highest degree of professionalism’, there was only silence from the players on social media.

Many of them are on international duty, including Bruno Fernandes whose criticism of Carrick’s tactics after the Champions League defeat to Como proved so damaging.

Following the announcement of Carrick's dismissal none of his former players - including Bruno Fernandes - were quick to say their goodbyes publicly

Meanwhile, his would-be successor Mauricio Pochettino is set to face the media on Friday

Pochettino will inherit this squad of players once he has completed his duties as US national team coach with the upcoming CONCACAF Nations League double-header against Haiti.

The former Tottenham and Chelsea boss is due to speak at 2.15pm Friday ahead of the first leg in Miami on Saturday night when he will face questions over the United job for the first time.

Pochettino is expected to stay in charge for the second leg in Cincinnati in the early hours of Wednesday morning before flying to Manchester to meet the players and prepare for the crunch clash with Liverpool at Anfield a week on Sunday.

The US have been staying in Trilith, near their new training headquarters in Fayetteville south-west of Atlanta, where they were also based before the World Cup.

It’s a unique place designed for the film industry and built around the Trilith Studios which are the largest outside Hollywood. The ideal place for Pochettino to prepare for life at Old Trafford.

He has embraced the American lifestyle since he was appointed US coach in September 2024, a few months after leaving Chelsea, and will be sorry to leave.

Pochettino is said to have developed a love of bourbon whiskey, country music and Nashville, with Ella Langley’s Choosin’ Texas one of his favourite tunes.

He has admitted crying over Miracle, the movie about the US hockey team made up of college kids famously beating the Soviet Union to the gold medal at the 1980 Winter Olympics.

But the pull of Manchester United was always going to be too great, and very soon he will be swapping Trilith for Old Trafford.

#2642. 6 takeaways from Detroit Lions coordinator prior to Bucs game

Detroit Lions coordinators met with the media on Thursday in preparation for their big game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers this week. Here are six takeaways I had from Drew Petzing, Kelvin Sheppard, and Dave Fipp.

Kyle Juszczyk inspired how the Lions use Sam LaPorta

Recently, the Lions have utilized a lot of return motions with Sam LaPorta—where he'll be in motion in one direction during the snap, and suddenly change directions after the snap. Here's a good example from last week:

Petzing revealed that he was inspired by how the 49ers use fullback Kyle Juszczyk—someone Petzing worked with at Harvard—when putting LaPorta in that role.

"You have got to have somebody who's athletic, who can play on the move, who can live in the gray a little bit because it's not like when he's going in full motion, he knows exactly what the look is or exactly where everybody's lined up," Petzing said. "And I think Sam does such a good job of navigating that. And then there's pass game stuff that comes off of it, obviously, which Sam is elite at. So, I think that's kind of where it came from and why we feel like it really fits us and him as a player."

Here's Juszcyzk doing something similar (albeit with no pre-snap motion)—against the Lions—but building some of the pass game stuff Petzing was referring to.

Our own Al Karsten was one of the first to notice some incredible splits between the first and second half pass protection. In short, the Lions have been one of the worst pass protecting units in the first half and one of the worst in the second:

The Lions have allowed 21 sacks this season, and 18 of them have come in the first half. Petzing had several explanations for the phenomenon.

"A lot of it is we've really ended the last five or six games running the ball probably 70 to 75 percent of the game, which probably has a little bit of hand in that," Petzing said. "I think settling in is a part of that. I like to think that we wear on people and bring fatigue in the way that we play and the way that we go through a game. So, some of those things could certainly play into it. And then part of it's probably just chance, a little bit of both."

Tyleik Williams already one of the best nose tackles in football

If you were just box-score scouting, you may overlook the impact of Lions 2025 first-round pick Tyleik Williams. But the defensive tackle has taken his game to the next level, and Sheppard believes he's alreayd one of hte best nose tackles in the league who is still scratching the surface with his pass rushing abilities.

"I'm seeing one of the best nose tackles in the NFL right now. And things may not show up on the stat sheet but just turn on the tape and show me where an offensive lineman blocks him one-on-one and has success. Rarely to never," Sheppard said. "And credit to him because he does have a lot more in his toolbox, a lot more in his arsenal where he could be saying, 'Oh, I need more pass rush.' He's never done that. He's taken advantage of his ops. He knows where we need him for us to play collectively at a high level and he's doing it."

Despite his high level of play, Williams has only played in 301 defensive snaps, just under 50%. For reference, Day 3 rookie defensive tackle Skyler Gill-Howard is barely behind him at 288 snaps. That likely has to do with game situation, and the Lions facing more passing situations than run on defense. But even so, Sheppard expects Williams to see his playing time rise soon.

"Are we going to try to find more plays for him? Absolutely. He's one of our better players right now."

While D.J. Reed remains sidelined, the Lions have leaned heavily on Roger McCreary. Sheppard told an interesting story on why he's drawn to a player like McCreary—who has his share of doubters, as the Lions are now his third team in the last two seasons. McCreary asked Sheppard not to pigeonhole him as an outside cornerback or nickel—just given him an opportunity to win anywhere.

Now, after a strong couple of games in Detroit, the roles have reversed. Whereas McCreary was leaning on Sheppard to give him an opportunity, now Sheppard is leaning on McCreary to produce on Sundays.

"He's worked his tail off schematically, physically to do the things that we want done here the way that we do them. And he's doing it at a high level," Sheppard said. "This past month, he's been one of our best secondary players. He's been one of our best corners, honestly. And I lean on him now. The same way he leaned on me with that trust factor of, 'Where should I sign?' I'm leaning on him now, now that things are hitting the road and that's a player that I count on come Sunday and he's earned that trust."

Early in the year, Lions second-round rookie Derrick Moore was not getting many opportunities. After missing significant time in training camp, Detroit wasn't prepared to give him more than a situational role. Sheppard noted that Moore never complained, just put his head down and put in the work. His role subsequently increased not too long after.

Now, with Aidan Hutchinson out for the rest of the year, Moore will be leaned on more than ever, and Sheppard believes he's already rising to the occasion—starting with his two-sack performance last week after Hutchinson went down.

"When his opportunity comes, when you operate in that way, when you operate like that, you're never going to squander that opportunity when it comes because this is what he's been doing all along," Sheppard said. "It's just at a bigger sample size now. But I'm seeing a player that's playing faster and faster each week. And that was the biggest message to him. We know what he's capable of. It's just doing it at a high rate over and over at a consistent basis."

Given Hutchinson's injury and some noticeable slipping on the turn in Munich, Germany, some have criticized the groundskeeping at Allianz Arena for the Lions vs. Patriots game last Sunday.

Don't count Dave Fipp among them. He believes the conditions were quite similar to that of Lambeau Field.

"I feel like that field reminds me a little bit of Green Bay, like afternoon, evening game when the sun goes down in Green Bay gets a little bit slick, sort of similar," Fipp said. "If you wear the right footing, I don't think it's an issue at all. We had some guys change cleats early in the game because I think they felt like they were slipping around a little bit. You could see it on a takeoff on field block or rush or a takeoff on a punt rush or return. Some of those guys are in three point stances digging in. But, other than that, yeah, no factor. I mean, both sides are playing on it. I felt like the conditions were great. Yeah, I had no issue."

#2641. Anthony Edwards: 'I never wanted to have surgery,' no timeline for return

Anthony Edwards met with the media Thursday, but that doesn't mean he'll be back on the court later that night when the Timberwolves host the Knicks. When will he return?

"I have no clue. Whenever my knee tells me it's ready, I'll be ready," Edwards said in his first public words since he had arthroscopic surgery to clean up his right knee three weeks ago. The surgery is expected to keep Ant sidelined until around Christmas.

Edwards said he didn't really want to have the surgery, but had to after the pain got worse.

"I'm the type of guy, I never wanted to have surgery. I thought it would just, you know, go away. In the offseason it was actually good, like we was managing it pretty good, treating it, and it wasn't as swole. Then, as soon as the season kicked off it, I don't know what happened. It just flared back up like really bad. Then I was like, "Man, it's time"...

"It was good in [training] camp, like I said. I think after the Miami game it started to flare up, and then it went down a little bit after the Orlando game, so we thought we were going to be alright, but then after the back-to-back it was really bad, like painful to fly, so I'm like, "I gotta get it."

It's a small sample size, but Edwards arguably was playing the best basketball of his career to start the season, averaging 33.3 points, 4.8 rebounds and 3.5 assists per game while shooting 40% from 3-point range, all while the Timberwolves were 3-1.

Minnesota, behind LaMelo Ball, Ayo Dosunmu and the best defense in the league, has gone 5-2 since Edwards went out. Edwards recognized what is going on and said that when he returns he wants to fit in.

"I'm thirsty to come back, but not super fast because of how they're playing. I don't want to take them out of rhythm," Edwards said. "But I told them, when I come back, I'm not going to try to be who I usually am and try to ball hog and take all the shots. I'm just going to fit in where I get in – take a couple catch-and-shoots. When they need me, I'm there."

Edwards isn't just going to accept a role, he's an elite player, but Minnesota might be better — and a more dangerous playoff team — because of what they have learned while he is out.

#2638. Stephen A. Smith still not giving up on Rams reaching the Super Bowl

The Los Angeles Rams' Super Bowl odds have been on a steady decline since the start of the season, and understandably so. They opened the year as the favorites at +500 before dropping to +700 after starting the season 2-3. Still, they were the favorites at that point.

Entering their Week 11 bye, they now have the seventh-best odds at +1200. Despite the fact that they might not even make the playoffs, Stephen A. Smith isn't ready to give up on the Rams just yet.

He said on "First Take" Thursday that he's staying on the bandwagon and is picking Aaron Donald and Myles Garrett to play in Super Bowl LXI at SoFi Stadium in February.

"Two of their final three games are against Seattle," Smith said. "It's hard to imagine them being Seattle twice. Maybe once, but not twice. So you're looking at it from that standpoint. C.C.'s position makes much more sense. If I had to bet my money, I'd go with that, but I'm not jumping off the bandwagon. I'm picking Aaron Donald and Myles Garrett to be at SoFi for the Super Bow, dammit, and I'm staying on that bandwagon until further notice. Even though I did remember thinking about the Chicago Bears and saying, 'Yo, they might do it,' so we'll see."

It sounds like Smith isn't 100% on the Rams, but he still likes their chances – especially compared to the Packers and Seahawks. They have a brutally tough schedule to navigate in the next seven weeks, so reaching the playoffs will be no bargain. But if they can get healthy and the defense keeps playing the way it has, watch out.

No other teams will want to see the Rams in the playoffs. Not with the reigning MVP and Defensive Player of the Year on their roster.

#2637. Nikita Kucherov trade request: Five potential landing spots for the reigning NHL MVP

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

One of the greatest players in Tampa Bay Lightning history may soon be wearing a different jersey. According to Sportsnet, Nikita Kucherov has told the Lightning he won't sign a contract extension and has requested a trade.

Kucherov, a two-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Hart Trophy winner as league MVP, is one of the best players of his era. The 33-year-old just passed the legendary Steven Stamkos for the all-time franchise lead in points and has shown no signs of slowing down.

Just last season, Kucherov posted 44 goals and 86 assists en route to his second Hart Trophy win. His underlying numbers were even better with a five-on-five goal differential of plus-38 and an expected goals share of 57.0 percent. Only a select few players can drive play from the wing like Kucherov, and that makes him a unicorn of sorts.

Kucherov is in the final year of a contract that pays him $9.5 million per season, and with the salary cap rising rapidly, he's due for a gargantuan raise next summer. It sounds like Kucherov and the Lightning were too far apart on that number, so the superstar winger has shifted his focuse to a change of scenery.

It's important to note that Kucherov has limited trade protection in the form of a 10-team trade list, but that should be more than enough for the Lightning to find a suitable trade partner. With that in mind, let's take a look at five teams that would be ideal fits for Kucherov as he prepares for the next chapter of his illustrious career.

Right out of the gate, this is the most natural fit of all the potential landing spots. General manager Kent Hughes has done a superb job of locking down his young core on team-friendly contracts, and as a result, the Canadiens have nearly $30 million in projected cap space for next season. They also have a glaring need in their top two lines, and I'd say the reigning Hart Trophy winner would fill that role quite nicely.

Montreal's moment to strike is now. It's an ascendant team with a great salary cap situtation and assets to spend. It's time to make a splash, and this would be a tsunami. Just imagine Kucherov on a power play unit with Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Lane Hutson and Ivan Demidov. Kucherov would also be coached by former Lightning teammate Martin St. Louis, so a rapport would already exist between player and coach. I expect the Canadiens to do everything in their power to land Kucherov.

We already know the Wild are big-game hunting at forward because they've been heavily linked to former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin. If I were advising general manager Bill Guerin -- and I'm certainly not -- I would recommend Minnesota package whatever assets it has offered Detroit and redirect them to Tampa Bay. No, Kucherov is not a center,  and that's the Wild's biggest need.

However, Kucherov is a rare breed of winger in that he can drive play better than most first-line centers from the wing. Put him on a line with Kirill Kaprizov, and the only time opponents will touch the puck is when they're pulling out of the net.

With Quinn Hughes also on an expiring contract, acquiring Kucherov would be a risky move for the Wild. What if they give up premium assets only to lose Kucherov and Hughes next summer? I don't think fear can dictate Minnesota's decisions. The team has a top-two defenseman in the world on its roster right now, and it has the opportunity to acquire a top-five forward. Worry about next summer when the time comes. Go all in to win the Cup while you have a chance.

It was no secret that the Hurricanes were in on the Connor Hellebuyck sweepstakes but just missed out. So, if they can't get better at preventing goals, why not get much better at scoring them? Carolina doesn't exactly need any help offensively, but adding Kucherov would go a long way to helping the team repeat as Stanley Cup champions. Besides, Kucherov would provide another level of playmaking and finishing that the Canes don't currently have on their roster.

Carolina has a good chunk of cap space available already, and it wouldn't need to shed much in order to make room for Kucherov. The Canes also have some enticing young players on their roster that might appeal to the Bolts, and they have three first-round picks over the next two drafts. Why not take a shot at landing a superstar winger?

Similar to the Hurricanes, the Mammoth were in the mix to acquire Hellebucyk, and for good reason. The goaltending tandem of Karel Vejmelka and Sebastian Cossa has not been good, so Utah may have to outscore its problems until one of the goalies finds a groove. Offense may be the best defense for the Mammoth -- and if that's the case -- then Kucherov should be in the mix for the Norris Trophy. There is a great young core of forwards in Salt Lake City, and I think Kucherov would be a perfect fit alongside Logan Cooley, who is emerging as a franchise center.

Utah also has plenty of draft capital with which to work, and it's projected for just over $25 million in salary cap space next season. The Mammoth don't have any major pending free agents on their cap sheet, so they're a suitor capable of signing Kucherov to a long-term extension.

Allow me to get a little bold on the fifth and final destination. The Stars have already failed to sign 27-year-old winger Jason Robertson to a long-term extension once. The two sides agreed to a one-year deal worth $12 million prior to the season, but Robertson's future with the team is still very much in doubt. What if Dallas and Tampa Bay executed a true "hockey trade" -- one player for one player?

Dallas would get the better player in Kucherov, but there are no guarantees regarding an extension. The Stars are in win-now mode, and Kucherov could help them get over the Cup hump immediately. Tampa Bay would get a younger player in Robertson, and although he doesn't have the elite playmaking ability of Kucherov, he's still an exceptionally talented scorer. Perhaps the Bolts could get him to join the team's core and sign a multi-year contract. This deal could work for both sides.

#2636. Cowboys point/counterpoint: Setting goals for the rest of the season

While the Dallas Cowboys are far from eliminated as the potential winner of the NFC East, it really doesn't feel like they have much of a chance. They are 4-6 with seven games to go. To eventually win the East, they would have to really change the direction they have been heading.

So what do they face now? And what do they need to accomplish so we no longer feel like this season is just circling the drain? Our Tom Ryle and Sean Martin offer their ideas.

Tom – Well, the obvious thing is that they need to win games, but that is the obvious goal each and every time the team takes the field. Clearly, a loss to the 1-8 Titans would be a horrible sign. It is hardly beyond the realm of possibility, sadly. To me, this is about more than simply getting a W against a hapless team. They have to look in control and capable of playing a strong game from start to finish.

But then comes a much more important goal: They need to string wins together. And their next game against the badly depleted Philadelphia Eagles is arguably the last really favorable chance for that this year.

This is important. Under Brian Schottenheimer this year, the Cowboys have yet to accomplish back to back wins. There just seems to be a true lack of confidence on the team. Putting two together could go a long way to creating some. And if we are going to keep talking about getting to the playoffs as the NFCE representative, it would also get them to .500 and keep them in striking range of the current division leading New York Giants. Then we can see what they can do against some stiffer competition down the stretch.

Sean – The Titans have certainly been in a lot of games this season, Tony Pollard has had some monstrous games out of the backfield, and will have to love what he saw from his former team's defense against Christian McCaffrey, and they have yet another defensive minded head coach to scheme against Schottenheimer and try to have the upper hand. Plus, the Cowboys have played two other games against the AFC South, narrowly escaping with a win at the Houston Texans, and beating the Colts in a fashion that set us up for exactly what we saw in the latest loss.

So yes Tom, getting out of this game with a win is a solid enough goal, and one might even go as far as saying controlling it for four quarters like we'd want to see is a sign of progress to play the first complete game of the season. But, it's not a win against a conference opponent not in the NFC East, something Schotty is still searching for. How do you have any playoff viability if you can't beat anyone good in your own conference? It's not in any way a win against a quality opponent, and it has absolutely just as much of a chance to be forgotten about as every other win this season against those Texans, Colts, Commanders, and Eagles.

The Cowboys are playing so poorly they have a chance to sweep the Eagles for the first time since 2021, winning their second game of the week next week in order to do so, and still have it all be a footnote.

I guess if you want to circle back on one of these wins with the context we now have through ten weeks, beating a Commanders team that went on to beat the Giants team the Cowboys are still chasing at home is a decent result. But nobody will forget that Jayden Daniels was knocked out of the game, and nobody is getting away with moving the goalposts a country mile for this season along with that. From potential playoff contenders to happy to be in the mix with the… 5-3-1 Giants? I'm not buying it, and oh by the way the most glaring and obvious thing the Giants do better than the Cowboys to start having instant success is coach better under their new leadership.

Tom – Maybe that's another way to look at things. The Cowboys need to prove they can show they are a viable NFL franchise, one that can play a full sixty minutes and close out games. Those elements have been lacking all season, even in some of their wins. The team is so up and down, even from play to play. They will have a strong defensive stop on one play, maybe a sack or a run stuff, then give up a big gainer – usually, it seems, on third and long. And the offense is not exempt. They will have several good plays, then a couple of dropped passes or a breakdown in the blocking scheme, and Bryan Anger or Brandon Aurbrey will have to come out. And if things weren't bad enough, Aubrey is showing signs of having the yips, missing kicks we used to take for granted.

And that's one other way to consider it. This team just does not have one thing it can consistently hang its hat on. Even Dak Prescott will have several bad reps in a row and things will stall.

There isn't one fatal flaw on this team. There are a collection of things that are making it so hard to keep up with their competition. I don't know how they can start to heal these wounds, but it would certainly be nice to see at least one thing get cleared up. That just might be the real goal for them.

Oddly, the news of Christian Parker being forced to surrender play-calling duties to Mike Pettine is, for me, encouraging. At least it shows the owner sees the problem and is willing to do something. (Yeah, I don't think this was Schotty's call.)

Sean – For fans with one eye toward the offseason already, the only good news about what you said is that the team is putting themselves in a position where getting help for any position group in the offseason would be seen as a good move. The bad news is we know how this always goes. The Cowboys will have to prioritize one thing or the other, meaning they sell us on already being stable at some other position to do this, and then that very thing holds them back on gamedays.

Dak Prescott starting a streak with this Titans game of not only playing well but winning would be great, but by season's end if they still aren't a playoff team, we'll have to do it all over again in year 12 for Dak and hope for a third straight year of good health from him. The defense needs an answer for how not to waste Quinnen Williams and Joey Porter Jr. right now, but nobody has those answers.

I do also like the idea of Pettine having more overall control now, to run this defense through the front seven where the denser nucleus of talent has shown itself. Not just Williams playing like a game wrecker, but Shemar James and even Caleb Downs as a box player too. This is almost surely more stable ground to build something around than Christian Parker's preferred position groups, cornerback and safety, where the injuries have been rampant for years.

Still, I can't recall a time where both the present and the future feels so shaky for the Cowboys, or trust in the leadership that can get an organization through shaky times is so low. After all, Pettine has only been here since October, and now he's calling plays? I don't know if we're even grasping how much of a structural failure it takes to get to that point in any season.

Maybe they'll still win the NFC East and find the faintest something to hang their hat on? Who knows.

One thing I do know is that it's Brawl of the Wild week as Montana State hosts Montana in one of the best rivalries in college football, and I can't wait for that! Here's hoping it's not just a fun Saturday but a successful Sunday for our Cowboys as well, Tom. Thanks for chatting.

#2634. NWSL commissioner’s championship address: Growth, relocation, ‘Rodman Rule’ and more

WASHINGTON – Ahead of the 2026 NWSL Championship game between Washington Spirit and Kansas City Current at Audi Field on Saturday night, league commissioner Jessica Berman shared her annual end-of-the-year remarks with the media.

Berman focused her initial remarks on the league's rapid financial growth, rising attendance and television audience that has been expanding since 2022. She pointed to significant increases in franchise valuations, player compensation and stadium investment as evidence of the league's transformation over the past four years.

Total regular-season attendance has climbed from approximately 1 million in 2022 to more than 2.5 million in 2026, an increase of 154 percent, according to the league. In terms of television audience, there has been a 16 percent increase, where 2.5 million adults between the ages of 18 and 34 watched the NWSL on national television last season. Total viewing time among that audience rose by more than 20 percent. Fans also streamed more than 1 billion minutes of NWSL matches this season, up 30 percent year over year. During the playoffs, viewership among adults ages 18 to 34 increased 96 percent compared with the previous postseason.

"Our audience is getting younger," Berman said, "and this is exactly what is driving the interest of media partners and sponsors."

The NWSL is in a crucial crossroads as it continues to carry the momentum of historic growth, while soon entering both a World Cup year and one of the most congested years in league history. This is all while the league faces the potential of another historic media rights deal on the horizon and will cap an usual NWSL playoff season with a monumental NWSL Championship.

Here, The Athletic breaks down some of the biggest takeaways from Berman's address.

Berman focused on the growth and rising franchise valuations, but as expansion fees, franchise valuations and operating budgets climbed, some existing ownership groups are struggling to find the capital to keep pace with the league's ambitions.

The financial pressures associated with that growth became particularly apparent this week when Racing Louisville FC publicly acknowledged that it needs additional investment to remain competitive. "As the NWSL has grown, so have the financial demands of competing in the league. Additional investment is needed to support the club's long-term future and we are actively working through a process to sell," the club said in a statement on Tuesday, signaling it was pursuing a sale to keep up with the increasing costs of operating in the NWSL.

The announcement from the club came after months of rumors about a potential relocation sale, which Berman earlier this season said, while not ideal, was not out of the question. During her address on Thursday, Berman was asked repeatedly about Louisville's future and the possibility that a sale could result in the franchise relocating to another market.

"As most professional sports leagues in America have, we also have specific policies around relocation," Berman said, emphasizing that the league has established policies intended to discourage relocation and protect clubs' ties to their communities. According to Berman, those policies are designed to make relocation a last resort to encourage and incentivize owners to continue to invest. "Any consideration of relocation would have to go through our normal process," Berman said.

"We have the financial wherewithal to ensure that our teams are set up for success. And again, unprecedented sports. Not to speculate specifically about the Louisville transactions, we don't have any news to share today. But I am confident that with the league support, we'll be able to identify the capital we need to ensure that the club is set for success for the short, medium, and long term."

In terms of expansion, the league showed no sign of slowing down as it continues its rolling expansion. One of the biggest announcements the commissioner made was the location of the Challenge Cup. The league is taking the game to a neutral site again this year, to Austin, Texas.

"There has been interest in that market over the last several processes, and so bringing an event to a neutral site that is not an NWSL market is an opportunity for us to learn the fan base and test the appetite, whet the appetite of the market, and we'll be excited to see how they welcome the NWSL challenge out to Austin," Berman said.

Last year, the league hosted the Challenge Cup in Columbus, Ohio, and later awarded an expansion franchise to the ownership group of MLS's Columbus Crew, the Haslam family.

As should be expected, Washington Spirit forward Trinity Rodman and the High Impact Player rule was also a recurring theme in today's availability.

It was around this time last year that the league announced the creation of HIP, which allows teams to access an additional $1 million in funds to go over that year's team salary cap. The rule allowed the Spirit to keep Rodman in the league, who was a free agent in last year's offseason and attracting contract offers from leagues around the world that could offer far more money than the Spirit, which was limited by the league's cap.

"It's incredibly important for us to keep Trinity in this league," Berman said on Thursday. "The fact that she's competing in the championship again is poetic, given how far we've come and all the progress we've made."

The rule is often called "the Rodman rule," but has been used by teams to attract big-name players from Europe, including U.S. women's national team players such as Cat Macario and Lindsey Heaps. Teams, though, are only able to tap into HIP funds once they reach their cap.

The rule recently underwent a significant overhaul by erasing the highly-controversial player criteria that determined who qualified for those funds. The changes came after a multi-grievance settlement with the NWSL Players Association. Berman on Thursday called this a "mini negotiation" that added "a new addendum" to the league's existing Collective Player Agreement.

"We had to be confident that any changes we were making to the High Impact Player rule were still going to achieve our stated objective, and the objective was importantly not to just raise the cap, but actually to create a targeted, tailored solution that would put us in a position to compete specifically for elite players," Berman said. "We are confident this change will continue to do that."

Many critics of the Rodman rule, including the NWSL Players Association, questioned why the league could not have simply raised its Salary Cap. It would have saved the league, the PA and Rodman the headache of multiple grievances and months of arbitration. Berman on Thursday re-emphasized that existing parameters for the HIP rule keep the spirit of the original rule alive.

"There are specific parameters that ensure that the charge that goes to the salary cap requires that a player make an excess of a particular amount of compensation," Berman said. "It has to be 12 percent of the salary cap, and so you don't actually, as a club, get access to that additional million dollars unless a player makes an excess of, I believe, it's $420,000 in the 2026 season.

"With that as a guardrail, we're confident that it will still accomplish our stated objective to be able to use it as a tool in the club's tool belt to attract and retain top players, and it actually gives a lot of the discretion and control to the GMs to decide how they want to curate the roster based on their specific sporting philosophy."

Rodman represents the kind of star player that the NWSL wants to recruit and retain as the global market continues to grow more competitive with every passing year. This weekend, Rodman and the Spirit are vying to be the second team to win an NWSL Championship at home. Berman said the Championship was already a sellout, with some tickets still to be released ahead of the final, which would make this the seventh consecutive playoff sellout for the Spirit in recent seasons.

"It's our job to create a financially sustainable league that is built for the future, and it is also our job to compete in the global labor market for talent," Berman said, "and we'll continue to analyze how we're doing in that global labor market with the key metrics that we analyze each and every season to make sure that we're on our front foot to compete for the best players in the world."

One of those metrics, Berman said, will be the number of players the NWSL sends to next summer's World Cup – which, truly, would be a full circle moment for the league as it compares where it is now to where it was after the final whistle of the women's World Cup in 2023.

Next year will mark the busiest calendar the NWSL will ever have to navigate, between starting the season in February during Super Bowl weekend for the first time and pausing for several weeks next summer to accommodate the women's World Cup in Brazil.

Given the growth of international players in the NWSL in recent years, it's likely that a record number of NWSL players will be taking part. Once the year concludes, some players in the league will be preparing to compete in the first-ever women's Club World Cup, which is being staged across the United States as a test run for the World Cup in 2031.

"It is the first time that we're going to be playing matches in the month of February, and it's important to recognize why that is happening as a league that is the home to the best players in the world," Berman said. "We want to ensure that we actually pause for the entirety of the Women's World Cup. That's a strategic decision that we made back in 2023 that we were no longer going to put the best players in the world in the position to have to choose or to feel like they were being left out of their club competition, and so in order for us to shut down our league for what will be seven weeks, we need to pull forward the start of our season.

"The only other alternative would be to play midweeks, and that would just increase the congestion for players who are already feeling the pressure from having to play for club and country. This was really a decision in service of player health and safety and welfare to pull forward games, and we're excited to use it as an opportunity to reach new audiences."

Those new audiences, at least in February, will include taking advantage of the league's broadcast partnership with ESPN and ABC, who are hosting the Super Bowl. Berman has long expressed the league's interest in making the most of this opportunity for potential cross-programming during Super Bowl weekend, which will coincide with the start of their season.

A growing calendar means growing conversations around stadium availability, which proved a challenge in recent weeks for NWSL playoffs. Two teams in particular, Gotham FC and Spirit, were faced with headaches over where some of their biggest games of the year would be played because their usual home stadiums, Audi Field and Sports Illustrated Stadium, were scheduled to host other events during playoff weekends. Notably, neither team owns the stadiums they play in, which are both operated by clubs in Major League Soccer.

Gotham subsequently played its semifinal against the Current at the 5,000-seat Icahn Stadium on Randall's Island in Manhattan, after concerns over the playing surface, which hosted several events in the weeks leading up to Decision Day and the NWSL postseason, again something that was outside of Gotham's control.

"I don't think anyone was more frustrated or disappointed with that outcome than the NWSL," Berman said. "Obviously, we want our players and our game to be showcased on the biggest stages, and so as we think about solving this problem, we think about it both in a short term and a long-term lens.

"We are focused on identifying ways to either control or influence where we play. On the control side, of course, this is the reason that Boston and Denver were admitted into our league. They are building purpose-built stadiums, and when those open in the next couple of years, we will be in a meaningfully different place in terms of creating optionality across our league.

"In terms of influence, there are a lot of ways to make progress against that. One of the ways is shared ownership, and again, that's in large part what drove our expansion process with Atlanta and Columbus coming in. Having shared ownership with MLS teams that own their stadium gives us the opportunity to have more influence over our schedule, but also more creative solutions like what Gotham announced in their move to Eithad (Park), they have a strategic partnership with NYCSC, and again, that will give them more influence over their stadiums.

"But we should acknowledge that solving infrastructure problems for many leagues takes 50 to 70 years. We've been at this before. I'm incredibly proud of the progress we made, and it's clear we have more work to do."

The rapid growth of the league and women's soccer globally is also impacting player development efforts across the board. Berman acknowledged the league's need to invest in the talent pipeline as one of the top priorities. As part of these efforts, the league is launching the NWSL Player Development Rule, to strengthen the pathway to professional soccer for the next generation of players. The rule aims to create actual incentives for clubs to invest in identifying, developing, and retaining young talent, and it gives the clubs the flexibility to design their program in the way that makes sense with their sporting philosophies.

"We know that we have to prioritize the pipeline, not just the pipeline of players, but the pipeline of talent that supports the players in the daily training environment," Berman said. "One of the things that makes the United States so uniquely positioned in the global women's soccer landscape is the depth of that potential pipeline. We have nearly 400,000 girls playing high school soccer alone in this country. That level of participation, combined with the infrastructure that exists around the college game and the growing professional opportunities that exist in the U.S., gives us an enormous foundation to build on."

The league also announced a program to help develop executives. The NWSL Sporting Executive Leadership Program, a first-of-its-kind program invested in talent, curated and developed in collaboration with U.S. Soccer and FIFA.

"This new year-long initiative will provide sporting executives at our clubs with curated, specialized education, mentorship, and leadership development opportunities tailored around the unique demands of our league and the women's professional team," Berman said. "These are the leaders making critical decisions about how to build their rosters, develop talent, and create environments where players can thrive. And they're setting the standard across the world."

Haley Carter (Washington Spirit), Caitlin Carducci (Orlando Pride), Angela Mangano (Houston Dash), Jeff Agoos (Portland Thorns), Kelly Cousins (Utah Royals) and Domè Guasch (Boston Legacy) make up the inaugural executive class.

This article originally appeared in The Athletic.

#2632. Corey Seager landing spots: Six possible destinations with Rangers veteran on the trading block

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

A new star-quality trade candidate recently barged onto the scene in Major League Baseball. The Texas Rangers are reportedly fielding and considering trade offers for veteran shortstop Corey Seager.

The Rangers signed Corey Seager to a 10-year, $325 million deal prior to the 2022 season, and that splash signing played a leading role in the Rangers' 2023 World Series triumph. Seager was named MVP of that World Series, and during the regular season he enjoyed perhaps the best campaign of his standout career. Now, though, with the Rangers facing an uncertain future, they may be looking to unload Seager and the five years and roughly $155 million left on his pact.

It won't be simple. Seager is going into his age-33 campaign in 2027, and he suffered a downturn at the plate this past season (while still remaining a plus at the plate and in the field). As well, he's been injury-prone for much of his 12-year career. Over the last four years, he's averaged 111.5 games per season, and in recent times he's been limited by injuries to his thumb, hip, back, and both hamstrings. At his age and after such a long history of health issues, there's no reason to think that will change. Additionally, Seager can control the process. While his contract included a limited no-trade clause that allowed him to block trades to eight teams of his choosing, Seager has now earned "10 and 5" rights – i.e., he's spent at least 10 seasons in the majors and the last five with the same team – which means he has the right to block any trade.

All that said, Seager is no doubt appealing to teams in contending mode and in need of upgrades on the left side of the infield. He still has strong quality-of-contact indicators at the plate, and he's still an asset with the glove. It's easy to dream on that career OPS+ of 135 from the shortstop position and the fact that he was at peak, at least when he was on the field, as recently as 2025. The Rangers are also presumably willing to pay down a chunk of his remaining commitment in order to make a trade more tenable. As for Seager's druthers, it's possible he'd like to play out his contract for a team better positioned to deliver to him a third career World Series ring.

With all those considerations laid out, let's have a look at a handful of teams who may – or at least should – be kicking the tires on a Seager trade. We'll proceed in taut and suspenseful alphabetical order …

The Braves made it to the NLDS this past season and have made the playoffs in eight of the last nine years. For much of that time, though, they've struggled to find a reliable presence at shortstop. This past season, Atlanta shortstops combined to bat just .222/.280/.322, which is squarely in "unacceptable liability" territory. As well, the top two turn-takers at the position, Mauricio Dubón and Ha-Seong Kim, are both free agents.

Boston still has Trevor Story under contract through next season with a club option for 2028. However, Story, who soon turns 34, appears to be very much in decline, and that's in addition to his troubles staying healthy. This past season, he had an OPS+ of just 75 and was barely above replacement level overall. The Sox have signaled they're open to an upgrade at the position, and Seager would certainly be that.

Why not a headline-grabbing reunion in L.A.? Seager was a Dodgers lifer before he inked that big contract with Texas, and that level of familiarity – plus the Dodgers' ongoing excellence – could be alluring. The Dodgers could also use an upgrade in the middle infield. They could install Seager at short and shift Mookie Betts to second base, where he has significant experience. Or they could keep Betts at short, where he's adapted so very well, and let Seager transition to second – a marginally less taxing position that might even help him stay on the field. Tommy Edman, meanwhile, would transition back to a super-utility role. Either way, it's a compelling theoretical fit.

The Yankees have previously shown trade interest in Seager, so it's no great leap to think they still might be eyeing him from afar. Young George Lombard Jr. is the shortstop of the present and future in the Bronx, so Seager would likely need to be willing to shift to third base if a Yankees trade is to come to pass. The Yanks have already signaled they're ready for an upgrade over Ryan McMahon, who's been frankly terrible at the plate since being acquired from the Rockies. The lefty-swinging Seager doubtless would enjoy that short porch in right at Yankee Stadium.

Trea Turner is signed through 2033, but defensively he's become unplayable at the shortstop position. No surprise, then, that the Phillies are open to moving him, perhaps to the outfield, and finding someone else to man the critical position of short. Seager would be a needle-moving addition for lead operator Dave Dombrowski as he attempts to keep the Phils' contending window open for a bit longer. There's an argument that this would make the Philly lineup too left-handed, but the potential upgrade over what Turner provided them this past season makes it a worthwhile sacrifice.

The Jays had one of the worst offenses in all of baseball last season, and that lack of punch was the leading culprit in their tumble from the heights of 2025. Seager could be installed at short or second, and from there the Jays could shuffle infield incumbents Andrés Giménez and Ernie Clement. Indeed, Clement is perhaps at his most valuable when he's deployed as a heavily used multi-positional talent.

#2630. NFC Playoff Picture: How standings, playoff odds look after big wins for Vikings, Lions

NFC Playoff Picture: How standings, playoff odds look after big wins for Vikings, Lions appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

On one side of things, the NFC playoff picture looks brighter for the Minnesota Vikings. But it looks a little different for the Detroit Lions. Here is how the standings and playoff odds look after big wins for the Vikings and Lions.

The Vikings thumbed their nose at the Packers in a 30-10 beatdown. As for the Lions, they crushed the Patriots, but star defender Aidan Hutchinson suffered a season-ending ACL injury.

Let's take a look at the NFC standings as the season pushes past the halfway point.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

NFC West — 49ers 8-1, Seahawks 6-4, Rams 6-4, Cardinals 3-7

It has been a great run so far for the 49ers. Their offense has been terrific. And the defense has been good except for last week's embarrassing 40-burger they meekly surrendered to the Cowboys. That's a concern moving forward.

Star edge rusher Nick Bosa said the team won't let the defense ruin a Super Bowl run, according to 49erswebzone.com.

"Our coaches have reiterated the fact that you have to enjoy wins in the NFL, but we've been around long enough to know that, when you don't perform good enough, you're not going to be celebrating, high-fiving in the locker room," defensive end Nick Bosa said. "Obviously, it wasn't a great feeling for the defense. Not taking away how good of an offense that is, and when they're clicking on all cylinders, it's a really good unit, but obviously we want to be better.

"Self-inflicted wounds, not getting lined up, some [mental errors]. There's a lot of things. And then, obviously, execution in terms of winning pass rushes and putting the quarterback on the ground. Feeling like you're the weak link on the team is not a feeling that's going to sit well with us."

Meanwhile, the Seahawks are still finding their way. They've been without Sam Darnold off and on. But Drew Lock has filled in nicely. Getting Zach Charbonnet back on the field may push them back into more serious contention for a repeat dream.

In Los Angeles, injuries have derailed the season. This doesn't look like a Super Bowl team. Even with Myles Garrett back, the injuries to Puka Nacua and Davante Adams have stymied the offense. There's hope for their return. But can they reach the playoffs if they lose more than another couple of games?

As for the Cardinals, it's a matter of looking ahead to 2027.

NFC North — Lions 7-2, Vikings 7-2, Bears 7-2, Packers 6-4

Trying to find clarity in this division is tough. But for now, it looks like the Bears have a slight edge. They've bulked up the defense, and their offense is rolling. Adding Kyle Monangai back to the backfield makes it that much tougher for defenses.

Head coach Ben Johnson said the Bears' lukewarm 4.2 yards per carry is deceiving, according to NBC Sports.

"I don't see it as bigger chunk runs, necessarily. The yards per carry is a deceiving statistic in a lot of ways," Johnson said. "We run the ball a lot in the red zone. And when you're down there, a four-yard carry is really an explosive.

"We go off efficiency. And we're under 50 percent efficient running the ball. We set our bar higher than that. We want to be closer to 55 percent. So we've got some work to do, and all our guys know it."

The passing attack with Caleb Williams rolling has no limitations. This is a great offense, good enough to reach the Super Bowl if the defense cooperates.

As for the Lions, they might have the NFL's best offense. It's especially true if you consider balance. The Lions can crush defenses on the ground or in the air. If the defense can play marginally well, this team could make big postseason noise.

Head coach Dan Campbell said the team can't focus on the loss of Hutchinson, according to The Athletic.

"It's unfortunate," Campbell said. "I hate it for him. Certainly for us, being selfish. It's hard for us, too, just to swallow it right when it happens.

"It's gonna require a lot out of everybody. One guy cannot pick up the slack of Aidan Hutchinson. But we have enough here to weather the storm and rise above it, so we'll do that."

As for the Vikings, they have new life with Kirk Cousins under center. There is a legitimate path to postseason success.

Clearly, the Vikings have the best defense in the NFL. If that continues throughout the rest of the regular season, the Vikings have a great shot at pulling off a division championship. All Cousins has to do is keep the offense moderately competitive. He's proven through the years that he can do that.

NFC South — Panthers 4-5, Buccaneers 3-6, Saints 3-6, Falcons 3-7

It's hard to get excited about any of these teams. They all have major flaws, as evidenced by their records. But the team that appears to have the best shot is Carolina. One thing the Panthers must do is avoid the onslaught of penalties they've faced this year.

How bad is it? The Panthers are the league's most-penalized team and on pace to break the NFL records for penalties (163) and penalty yards (1,358). But head coach Dave Canales said he doesn't mind some of the penalties, according to The Athletic.

"If you're not getting penalized at all, you're not playing hard enough," Canales said. "What I'm talking about is pre-snap. I'm talking about post-snap. Those are the things that we have to figure out, that we have to clean up. And there are things that we're working (on) to do that.

"Some of those judgment calls, I got a little frustrated just because I want our guys to be able to play physical and be aggressive, and not have to worry about those types of things."

Meanwhile, the Buccaneers have played good defense at times this year. They lead the NFL in takeaways. But they haven't found the mesh between offense and defense that has allowed them to win games consistently.

Head coach Todd Bowles said the offense has the ability to get things done, according to joebucsfans.com.

"Well, we're running the ball pretty [well]," Bowles said. "You know, obviously, everybody has got to gel together at the same time, and there [are] going to be mistakes.

"It's not all coaching. It's players as well. We've got to do a better job getting the plays into them and calling them; they've got to do a better job of executing them. But we got better in the run game, and we got that part down. Now we're just trying to catch up the passing game with it."

What about the Saints? Do they have a real say in this? Because of their sporadic performances, it's hard to see them as a real contender. They scored very well early in the season, but have totals of only 10, 22, and 17 over the last three games.

Still alive, the Falcons simply haven't shown anything to make themselves look like a real contender. They blew out Green Bay and stumped the 49ers. But pretty much everything else has been a frustrating mess. And over the past three weeks, they've totaled only 30 points.

NFC East — Giants 5-3-1, Cowboys 4-6, Commanders 3-5-1, Eagles 2-7

Even though the Giants have a three-game lead in the loss column, it's hard to see them as having firm control of the division. Looking at the upcoming schedule, that lead will likely shrink quickly. That's not a good look for a division leader.

The call has been made for head coach John Harbaugh to be more aggressive to give the Giants a chance to hang on to their division lead, according to The Athletic. Harbaugh didn't go for it on fourth and inches against the Commanders.

"That would have been gutsy — ballsy," Harbaugh said the day after the game. "We could have gone for that one. And you know, I'm kind of kicking myself. Maybe we should have just gone for that one, too."

Later, the Giants again didn't go for it.

"When we were talking about it during the game, we just felt like they were out of our range to go for (it)," Harbaugh said. "A lot of it was the analytics too, but even just the feeling comfortable about doing it because we have a chance to pin them back in there."

It makes sense to say the Giants have to be aggressive down the stretch. That's their only chance of holding off the Cowboys.

As for the Cowboys, they're hoping the recent chance of giving the play-calling duties to Mike Pettine. If they can get the defense somewhat stabilized, they still have a shot. Pettine said there's no magic bullet, according to dallascowboys.com.

"One thing I learned a long time ago is football's a game of a million little things," Pettine said. "There's no one magic play to run. It's a lot of the detail stuff. Just been taking a lot of notes. It's not like it's something that, 'Hey, we're going to do these 30 things different today,' but it's things that need to get addressed.

"I think I got a pretty good feel now for the roster. Part of the plan needs to be, 'Hey, let's highlight what we do well,' and make sure we gear that towards taking away just typical game plan stuff, take away what the opponent does well. It's a lot of little things."

As for the Commanders, they are still within shouting distance. And they have the tiebreaker advantage over the Giants. Plus, their schedule down the stretch has opportunities for victories. However, they have failed many times in late-game situations. So, it's hard to get on board with the Commanders making a dramatic turnaround.

As for the Eagles, they're the only other team in the same boat as the Cardinals. Season over. Look toward 2027.

The 49ers are the overwhelming favorite to claim the No. 1 overall seed. They have a 65% chance going into Week 11, according to ESPN. There's a big drop to the Vikings at 17%. The only other realistic chances come from the Lions (10%) and Bears (7%).

In terms of making the playoffs, the 49ers are at 99% and the Vikings are 97%. They are followed by the Lions (90), Bears (86), and Buccaneers (62).

Floating near the 50-50 line are the Seahawks (49), Rams (45), Giants (44), and Cowboys (43). The Packers roll in at 33, followed by the Panthers at 32. On the fringe, the Commanders are at 14.

#2629. MLB rumors: Yankees eye Alec Bohm, Tarik Skubal books more meetings, plus Nationals, Red Sox, Mariners, more
