The uncertain 2026-27 Major League Baseball offseason is fully underway. The ongoing CBA negotiations and the near certainty of an owner-implemented lockout on Dec. 1 loom over all, and it may indeed mean a flurry of trades and free agent signings leading up to that date. That was certainly the case leading up to the last lockout of 2021-22. As for the present moment, the General Manager Meetings in Las Vegas are underway, and since there may not be any Winter Meetings this offseason (thanks to the lockout), the GMs' pow-wow could instead be a locus of activity.

Thanks to that prospect of a hastened pace and the ongoing GM Meetings, offseason rumors are flowing. Speaking of which, we'll be here each day to round up what's out there. You can find Wednesday's supply just below.

The Red Sox are once again shopping outfielder Jarren Duran, reports the Boston Globe. He has been in trade rumors constantly the last two years or so. Boston has also reportedly shown interest in free agent Seiya Suzuki, the best right-handed bat on the market. With Gold Glover Wilyer Abreu entrenched in right, the Red Sox would presumably use Suzuki in left field or DH.

Duran, 30, has two years of team control remaining and he's a possible buy-low candidate. From 2023-25, he authored a .276/.339/.471 batting line with 17 homers and 32 steals per season. He slipped to .207/.266/.361 in 2026, however, and the Red Sox need to add power and get more right-handed. Moving Duran to clear a spot for Suzuki would address both needs.

The New York Yankees are eyeing an upgrade at third base given the prolonged struggles of Ryan McMahon, and free agent Alec Bohm may be a potential target for GM Brian Cashman, according to the New York Post. Bohm, 30, is coming off a subpar walk year for the Philadelphia Phillies, but he has a career OPS+ of 101 overall. He also fared much better in the second half, and his season-long numbers were dragged down by a terrible April. Bohm is not much of a fielder these days, but the Yankees may be willing to live with that if they determine he can provide an offensive upgrade.

As for McMahon, Cashman already conceded to looking for a replacement.

"He's signed through next year for us, but I definitely know we need to improve production in a lot of different spots on the club if we can," he told reporters on Tuesday. "So we'll be open-minded to finding what we can run into if it's there."

The market for ace Tarik Skubal, far and away the top free agent available this offseason, continues to pick up steam, and it may be that he signs his next contract before the owners lock out the players on Dec. 1. The Los Angeles Dodgers, who traded for Skubal leading up to the deadline, the New York Mets, the Chicago Cubs, and the San Diego Padres are known to have varying levels of interest in Skubal. Now, the New York Post reports, the Toronto Blue Jays have entered the fray and emerged as Skubal suitors.

As for the Dodgers, they indeed plan to meet with Skubal, GM Brandon Gomes said. There could be a twist in their pursuit, though; The Athletic reports that the Dodgers are interested in Skubal on a short-term deal, presumably with a higher AAV like they gave to Kyle Tucker. But given the uncertainty of the CBA, would Skubal be willing to sign a contract that has him back on the market in just a few years?

Mets top executive David Stearns, meanwhile, emphasized on Tuesday that he and the club are willing to offer lengthy contracts to pitchers but that circumstances matter. That, in theory, should allay fears that he's not prepared to make a significant offer.

The San Diego Padres not long ago declined their club option on right-handed starter Nick Pivetta. However, they may not mean a parting of ways for club and player. Padres lead decision-maker AJ Preller on Tuesday told reporters, including Marty Caswell, that the team hopes to work out a new agreement with Pivetta so that he can return to San Diego for the 2027 season and perhaps beyond. Pivetta enjoyed a standout season in 2025, but his 2026, while excellent while on the mound, consisted of just eight regular-season starts because of elbow problems.

Dylan Crews, the 24-year-old outfielder for the Washington Nationals, has yet to reach the potential that made him the No. 2 overall draft pick in 2023. However, that ceiling is still there, and Crews is obviously young enough to realize his promise. Speaking of Crews, the Athletic reports that multiple teams have approached the Nats about Crews' availability in trade and that the Nats have not declared him off-limits. That of course doesn't mean a trade will happen, but a change of scenery for Crews may indeed be a winter possibility.

Outfielder Randy Arozarena was the Seattle Mariners' top player last season, and now he's a free agent. The M's, though, may not be interested in bringing back Arozarena and instead may be targeting fellow free agent outfielder Seiya Suzuki, the Seattle Times reports. Each veteran outfielder will be going into his age-32 season in 2027, and each produced at a high level in 2026.

After missing the playoffs in back-to-back seasons and trading away catcher Adley Rutschman leading up to the 2026 deadline, the Baltimore Orioles seem like a teardown candidate on paper. However, president of baseball operations Mike Elias batted down talk of a major roster makeover. "A lot of our key, core players are very unlikely to go anywhere," Elias told the media, including the Baltimore Banner, at the GM Meetings.

That presumably means that coveted shortstop Gunnar Henderson, among other notable names, won't be going anywhere this winter.

#2628. France star Desire Doue is left with gruesome tooth injury after PSG youngster suffered elbow smash to the face during Les Bleus' dismal defeat by Italy

Published: 06:41 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 07:35 EST, 13 November 2026

France star Desire Doue was left with a loose front tooth after being hit with a nasty elbow in France's 3-1 defeat to Italy in the Nations League.

The PSG winger was left in need of some emergency dental work by Italy's Davide Frattesi who caught the 21-year-old in the mouth while shielding the ball.

In his post match interview French boss Zinedine Zidane, when asked if Doue had lost a tooth, replied: 'Yeah I think so. We’re going to take him straight there, a tooth has come loose I think, we’ll take care of him starting tomorrow.'

It was a poor day all round for the Frenchman who not only had his tooth dislodged but was also unable to impact a poor game for Les Blues in which the Azzuri beat them at the San Siro.

To compound Doue's misery it was the offender Frattesi who scored Italy's second goal in the 3-1 win just six minutes before he performed some unorthodox dentistry.

The Lazio midfielder's goal completed the Italians' comeback after going 1-0 down to a Michael Olise goal just ten minutes in before Inter Milan's Francesco Esposito levelled things up just 16 minutes later.

Desire Doue was left with a loose front tooth after receiving an elbow in the mouth from Davide Fratessi

Fratessi got away with just a yellow card as Italy beat the French 3-1 at the San Siro

Frattesi gave Italy the lead early on in the second half before Esposito netted his second from the spot to put the game out of reach.

Speaking after the game Zidane was surprisingly positive about his team's performance despite the loss, saying that losing is, 'part of the process.'

The French then went onto say: 'The most important thing is creating chances. Hitting the post had an impact, but I'm not disappointed.

'I would have been if we hadn't created good possession. What we need to analyse is why we weren't at the right level off the ball.'

The World Cup winner was not entirely positive however, later saying: 'in the second half we ran into difficulties, especially defensively.'

The victory put Italy level on points with the French in Group A with both sides having won three drawn one and lost one.

But France will have an opportunity to right their wrongs and return to the top of the group on Sunday as they welcome Turkey.

But if Italy beat Belgium on the same day the French will have to settle for second.

#2626. Cam Schlittler named American League Cy Young winner: Yankees ace wins in just second MLB season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Yankees ace Cam Schlittler is the winner of the American League Cy Young Award for 2026. Schlittler was a unanimous selection via the Baseball Writers Association of America balloting, the results of which were announced on Wednesday, beating out Blue Jays ace Dylan Cease and Guardians rookie Parker Messick.

Schlittler's win snapped the run of free agent Tarik Skubal, who won the last two AL Cy Youngs as a member of the Detroit Tigers.

This past season, the right-handed Schlitter in his age-25 campaign put up dominant numbers:

In addition to the above, Schlitter led AL pitchers in WAR with a mark of 7.0, and his ERA+ of 215 also paced his league. That 215 ERA+, which means that Schlittler's park-adjusted ERA was 115% better than the league average, is a Yankees franchise record. Among Yankee qualifiers, only Ron Guidry's 208 in 1978 comes close. Additionally, Schlittler tied for the AL lead this season with an FIP of 2.56, and he struck out 31.4% of opposing batters, which also ranked second in the AL.

Without Schlittler's top-shelf contributions, the Yankees, without franchise slugger and reigning back-to-back AL MVP Aaron Judge for almost 100 games, might have struggled to make the postseason. Instead, Schlittler's excellence at the front of the rotation helped them win 93 games, post the AL's top run differential, and advance to the ALDS.

"Cam had as dominant a season as a starting pitcher can have from start to finish," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said in a statement. "He's shown an astonishing amount of growth since we drafted him, and his success is no accident. Cam has a tireless appetite for hard work and refinement that has allowed his talents to truly flourish. This Cy Young is richly deserved. Cam was the most dominant pitcher in our league and continues to grow into a foundational player for this franchise."

While Schlittler was outstanding as a rookie in 2025, this past season, he increased usage of his sinker and cutter and improved ride on his 98-mph fastball helped him take the next step and become one of the very pitchers in all of baseball. Since Schlittler doesn't turn 26 until February, continued dominance may be on the way.

Schlittler is now the seventh Yankee to win the Cy Young Award. He joins teammate Gerrit Cole in 2023, Roger Clemens in 2001, Guidry in 1978, Sparky Lyle in 1977, Whitey Ford in 1961, and Bob Turley in 1958.

#2624. Reid Draws The Line On Kelce’s Desire To Play Through Pain

Andy Reid is making the hard calls to protect his veteran tight end, even when Travis Kelce begs to take the field. The Chiefs head coach has made it clear that Kelce's willingness to play through a high ankle sprain will not override medical reality. While the star tight end says he is ready to play, Reid is setting a limit to protect the team's most reliable target.

The tension between a player's heart and a coach's duty played out clearly during the recent matchup against Atlanta. Kelce reaggravated his injury on a 23-yard catch-and-run on the opening drive, yet he was fully ready to return for more action. "He wants to play. He wants to practice every play. He wants to play every play," Reid said regarding the tight end's mindset, according to a report. The player himself echoed this sentiment on the November 18 episode of his podcast, stating, "I'm ready to rock and roll this week." Kelce went further, noting that "if I'm out there on a good ankle or a bad ankle, it doesn't [expletive] matter to me." That kind of grit usually wins games, but Reid sees the bigger picture.

Reid knows that letting a 37-year-old veteran play on a twisted ankle is a gamble the Chiefs cannot afford to take. "I want to make sure that thing doesn't get worse," Reid said, explaining his decision to keep Kelce on the sidelines while the team was already winning 35-13. The coach sees a player who thinks he is still young, noting bluntly, "He thinks he's still 20." Reid's approach involves risking short-term frustration to preserve the offense's long-term health.

Despite the injury scare, Kelce returned in the second quarter and practiced fully on Wednesday, showing he is healing well. "He's doing well now. He's running around," Reid confirmed, though he remains cautious about the workload. The tight end has been managing this right ankle issue since the Week 6 victory over the Los Angeles Chargers, adding to the complexity of the situation. Kelce described his own motivation simply: "I love playing this game" and "I signed up for this thing to be out there putting my heart on the line and my body on the line for my teammates." The Chiefs face the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday, Nov. 22, at 1 p.m. ET at Arrowhead Stadium.

#2623. National League Reliever of the Year: Matt Snyder explains his 2026 BBWAA ballot

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Mason Miller of the Padres won the 2026 National League Reliever of the Year award on Wednesday evening. That wasn't all too surprising, but I still wanted to explain the thought process behind my ballot. This was an honor, as it was the first-ever Baseball Writers' Association of America award for a relief pitcher. Yes, there have been plenty of reliever awards over the years, but this was the first year the BBWAA handed out such hardware.

1. Mason Miller, Padres2. Jhoan Duran, Phillies3. Adrián Morejón, Padres4. Trevor Megill, Brewers5. Mason Montgomery, Pirates

And now here's how it unfolded on my end.

First off, I didn't even bother to look at win-loss record. It's a flawed enough stat these days with any individual player, but we really shouldn't be judging relievers by it. I'm also not worried about team performance here, as this is an individual award and we don't even need to wrestle with the word "valuable" being in the title like some MVP voters might. This is simply, "Who was the best relief pitcher in the league?"

What makes the best relievers? Run prevention (ERA, FIP, xFIP, etc.) matters, as does keeping runners off base (WHIP). It's helpful not only to the defense to strike hitters out, but it can also help a reliever bail out his team, so that's going to matter. Workload matters as well, as a reliever eating up as many outs as possible is very valuable to a team. I didn't factor saves as much as keeping leads (blown saves can hurt). Something I find helpful in judging relievers is win probability added. A reliever blowing games is going to be dinged in a big way, while closing down tougher games (one-run leads as opposed to three) is going to score extra via this measure. It's trickier with relievers, but WAR can help tell a story here, too.

Finally, I have no doubt there was some eye test involved. That is, when I'm watching a game, which reliever coming out of the bullpen feels the most imposing to the opposition. Miller, Duran and Megill especially got bonus points here.

A quick rundown of the major stats I examined follows.

Among NL relievers, Miller was the best in ERA (1.67), xERA, FIP, xFIP and several other categories. Duran was second in ERA (and xERA, FIP and xFIP) with Yuki Matsui third, Brandyn Garcia fourth and Abner Uribe fifth. Megill was third in FIP, while Montgomery was third in xFIP and Morejón was fourth.

In terms of keeping runners off base, Garcia led NL relievers in WHIP; Megill was second, Miller third, Duran ninth and Montgomery 10th.

Kudos to Garcia for the excellent season, but his workload (51 ⅓ innings) dinged him a bit. Speaking of, Morejón worked 86 innings compared to 70 from Miller, 63 ⅔ from Montgomery, 61 ⅔ from Megill and 59 ⅓ from Duran.

That said, Garcia, Matsui and Uribe are firmly in the mix through these categories.

Miller crushes here. He struck out 129 hitters, giving him 16.6 K/9 and a 47.4 K%. Montgomery was second in strikeout rate at 37.7%. Yes, it was that much of a blowout for Miller. Duran was third at 35.6%. Garcia was sixth, Morejón ninth, Megill 14th, Uribe 25th and Matsui 28th.

Miller tied for the league lead in saves with Riley O'Brien. I never considered O'Brien, as his ERA was north of 4.00.

Miller was also 38 of 41 in save chances. Duran was 33 of 35. Megill had 30 saves and seven holds with only three blown saves. Montgomery had 18 saves and nine holds with three blown saves. Morejón blew five saves, but he had three saves and 28 holds with an awful lot of multi-inning appearances. Uribe had six saves and 23 holds with two blown saves. Garcia? Stellar. He closed down five saves and 18 holds without ever blowing a lead. Matsui never blew a lead either, but he only had one save and 10 holds, meaning he wasn't tasked with much in the way of high-leverage innings. Being teammates with Miller and Morejón (and Jasaon Adam and Bradgley Rodríguez) will do that. As such, along with his relatively low strikeout rate, we can safely eliminate Matsui.

By the time I've gotten here, I have seven players for five spots: Miller, Morejón, Duran, Megill, Montgomery, Uribe and Garcia.

Using the FanGraphs calculation, Miller leads the way by a country mile at 3.7. Duran is second at 2.9, with Morejón at 2.8 and Megill at 2.5. Montgomery is eighth, Uribe ninth and Garcia, due in part to the workload concern, down at 17th.

Over on Baseball Reference's version, Duran actually leads the way at 3.4. Miller is next at 3.1, followed by Montgomery (2.4) and Uribe (2.3). Megill sits at 1.7 while both Morejón and Garcia are at 1.9.

In WPA, yes, Miller leads the way again at 4.56. Uribe is second at 3.49, with Morejón third at 3.23, Montgomery fourth at 2.86, Megill seventh, Garcia eighth and Duran 11th.

Miller in first place wasn't all too difficult. He was the best relief pitcher in baseball in 2026 and checked every single box.

I had trouble with Duran over Morejón, while Megill and Montgomery were also very close in that group, as were Uribe and Garcia. I ended up leaning on Duran's high strikeout rate and excellent run prevention, which helped clear the way for his lead in WAR. Morejón's workload meant I couldn't go any lower than third with him, given how many important outs he soaked up for the Padres. Megill's regular-season numbers were better than Uribe's, notably the under-the-hood numbers, even if they were very close. And Montgomery was an absolute beast for the Pirates.

It was incredibly tough to leave Uribe off, and Garcia was my hard-luck seventh-place finisher here when I had only five spots on my ballot.

#2620. Padres' Mason Miller, Blue Jays' Louis Varland named MLB Relievers of the Year in first-ever BBWAA award

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

San Diego Padres closer Mason Miller and Toronto Blue Jays closer Louis Varland have been named the winners of the first-ever Baseball Writers Association of America Reliever of the Year award. The BBWAA introduced the award this year and, moving forward, will hand it out annually along with Rookies and Managers of the Year, Cy Young, and MVPs.

The BBWAA's Reliever of the Year award is separate from the Mariano Rivera Award and Trevor Hoffman Award, which honor the best relievers in the American League and National League, respectively. The Rivera and Hoffman Awards replaced the Delivery Man of the Year Award in 2015 and are voted on by a panel of former relievers, including Rivera and Hoffman.

Like the other BBWAA awards, the new Reliever of the Year award is voted on by BBWAA members (two per MLB city in each league). Votes were submitted before the beginning of the playoffs, meaning that only regular-season contributions are taken into account.

The best closer in baseball is the first-ever BBWAA National League Reliever of the Year. Miller was overwhelming from start to finish this past season, pitching to a 1.67 ERA with 129 strikeouts in only 70 innings. He led all pitchers with 3.9 WAR, well ahead of second-place Louie Varland (3.1 WAR), and he led the NL in saves (38) and games finished (57).

Miller's strikeout rate lapped the field. Here are the highest strikeout rates (strikeouts per batter faced) among qualified relievers:

Miller just completed his first full season with the Padres. He was acquired from the Athletics at the 2025 trade deadline at a very high cost: San Diego sent shortstop Leo De Vries, one of the best prospects in baseball, to the A's in the six-player deal. Miller has been worth the price, though. He owns a 1.45 ERA in parts of two seasons with the Padres.

This is the first major award of Miller's career, who finished fourth in the 2024 AL Rookie of the Year voting and has two All-Star Game selections (2024 and 2026), but otherwise had never received Cy Young or MVP votes prior to this season. He beat out the Brewers' Trevor Megill and Phillies' Jhoan Duran for the award.

After jumping into the national spotlight with his high usage during the 2025 postseason, Varland is the first winner of the BBWAA American League Reliever of the Year award. His 1.27 ERA led qualified relievers and his 3.1 WAR was tops in the AL. Varland struck out 87 batters in 78 innings and was fifth with 35 saves. He won with his sheer dominance, not his saves total.

Varland was a workhorse for the Blue Jays this year, much like he was last October. He finished second in saves of at least four outs during the regular season:

The Blue Jays acquired Varland from the Minnesota Twins, his hometown team, at the 2025 trade deadline. He struggled initially after the deal, posting a 4.94 ERA with Toronto after the deadline, but Varland found his footing in the postseason and then found another gear in 2026. He was one of the game's best relievers and a true workhorse.

Varland was an All-Star for the first time this season. This was also his first year receiving any award votes. He beat out the Guardians' Cade Smith and Rays' Bryan Baker for the award.

Lionel Messi remains the highest-paid player in Major League Soccer with $28.3 million in guaranteed compensation, according to a salary release Thursday by the players union, with Chicago's Robert Lewandowski second.

Argentine legend Messi topped the league list revealed by the MLS Players Association with compensation almost $8 million higher than last year, although his figures include only playing compensation and did not include income from other sources.

Messi signed a contract extension through 2028 last year.

Poland's Lewandowski, who joined the Chicago Fire earlier this year, was second overall with $19.51 million followed by Orlando's Antoine Griezmann of France at $13.938 million, South Korean star Son Heung-min of Los Angeles FC at $11.152 million and Swiss international Breel Embolo of Atlanta United at $10.81 million.

Among MLS clubs, Miami topped all teams in total guaranteed compensation at $59.37 million with Chicago second on $41.29 million, Atlanta third on $38.35 million, the Los Angeles Galaxy fourth on $34.91 million and LAFC fifth on $32.91 million.

The league's lowest total team compensation was Philadelphia Union at $12.64 million with Sporting Kansas City second lowest at $13.30 million and DC United third lowest at $14.55 million.

The figures are through October 9 and are annualized for players who arrived in the summer transfer period.

#2618. Why England were unremarkable on Harry Kane's big night, the Ben White problem - and established star whose place could be under threat from Morgan Rogers, writes IAN LADYMAN

Published: 02:00 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 07:49 EST, 13 November 2026

England will head to Spain on Sunday for a Nations League shoot out with the World Champions. A win in Madrid could see Thomas Tuchel's team progress to the quarter-finals next March as group winners.

It wasn't always easy on Harry Kane's big night at Wembley against Croatia, though. Indeed this was probably England's worst performance since losing to Argentina in the World Cup semi-final last July.

Here Daily Mail Sport looks at the key issues emerging from last night's tight squeeze.

Self-defeating abuse of White is madness and must stop

In case nobody has noticed, England are not over stocked with competent right-backs.

Trent Alexander-Arnold isn't wholly trusted in big games by Thomas Tuchel, Reece James is always injured and Tino Livramento has also struggled to be available. Why, then, is a significant section of the England support so determined to drive Ben White away from the international scene?

White plays for Arsenal, the champions of England. He is a fine, versatile defender who would be gratefully received and appreciated by fans of most national teams in world football. He had issues with the previous England management regime and does not apologise for that.

Ben White was booed when he came on. The abuse towards the defender must stop

He spoke about it this week and made it clear he didn't wish to reopen old wounds. All that matters now is that he is willing and available. But – despite a plea from Tuchel before this game – England fans still booed him when he came on as a substitute last night.

It's a disgraceful way to treat a footballer who can be an asset to his country going forwards and it's something the England manager cares deeply about. Do we want to win the next Euros or not? Do we want our best players motivated and driven and part of the squad? Or do we want to faff about harbouring old grudges related to a situation in Qatar four winters ago that none of us really know that much about?

The choice is clear. If we are not careful, we will drive a good footballer away from the England set-up for good. It's madness.

Big night for Kane but questions for England

They came to celebrate Harry Kane and the England captain got his goal. Number 92 for the striker. Beneath all the fuss over England's talisman, however, this came perilously close to being a step backwards for Thomas Tuchel's England.

The England manager has been saying since the last international break in September and October that he wanted his team to go to Madrid on Sunday in with a shout at knocking Spain from the top of this Nations League Group. Had Croatia been a little smarter in front of goal at Wembley last night, England would have been heading for a dead rubber against the world champions.

Harry Kane scored on his big night as England edged out a 2-1 win over Croatia at Wembley

It was a night to remember for Kane as he was honoured after receiving his record 126th cap

Three times in the last ten minutes of this game, Croatia had good opportunities to score a second goal and take a point from the game that would have been perfectly justified. So England crawled over the line but there was little here that was impressive with questions emerging once again about how capable really are when they don't have the ball.

Kane put it well himself afterwards when he said: 'You can't always expect things to be perfect. Of course, we know we can improve on a few bits and we will need to if we want to win on Sunday.'

Tuchel himself will perhaps have quiet concerns. One of the German's worries about this England team is that they sometimes struggle to take training performances on to the field and this was another case in point.

The ultimate target for this team is to win the home Euros in 2028 and the pressure will need handling in front of their own supporters if they are to do that. With that in mind, it's good to know that the FA are interested in hosting the finals of this Nations League competition next summer.

If England make it through next March's two-legged quarter-finals, they could do with some practice of playing high-stakes games at Wembley.

Asked last week on the day he announced his squad whether Jordan Pickford was still his number one goalkeeper, Tuchel was unequivocal.

'He is,' said Tuchel. 'But the competition is on there as well. Like for the outfield players. And James Trafford will get regular starts now, that's what we wanted. They shared the matches last time. There's an opportunity that we maybe do this again.'

Morgan Rogers impressed after opening the scoring inside the opening half-an-hour

Jordan Pickford starting against Croatia could lead to James Trafford playing against Spain

With all this in mind, it was expected that Trafford would start this game with Pickford getting the gloves for the one that really matters in Spain on Sunday. That wasn't the case, so we wait with interest to see what the England manager does in Madrid.

What nobody really wants is for a return to the situation we had in the 1980s when Ron Greenwood used to rotate between the late Ray Clemence and last night's guest of honour Peter Shilton.

England's back four is the one area of this team that can look unconvincing – they did again last night - and the last thing they need is not to know who their goalkeeper is from one match to the next. Tuchel is going to have to make a decision.

Interesting that Tuchel chose to put Dan Burn into his team for this game, despite the Newcastle defender not being in the original squad.

With Marc Guehi and Ezri Konsa both absent with injuries, Everton's Jarrod Branthwaite would have expected to play on the left of Jarell Quansah here. Instead, Burn leapfrogged him in the queue and maybe we should have paid more attention to something Tuchel said the day before the game.

'Jarrad Branthwaite is doing very well but it's a very different style of play for him from Everton towards us,' said Tuchel.

Jarrad Branthwaite clearly has a way to go before he's fully trusted to start by Thomas Tuchel

'You can see that Dan Burn is straight away a big voice in training and is more used to the style with Newcastle from the last two seasons with Eddie Howe where they followed in a high press and to man-man. And of course he was with us at the World Cup so he is used a bit more to our style of play.'

That's all very well and logical but – that being the case – why was Branthwaite chosen ahead of Burn in the original group of 25 last Friday? Burn, as it happened, had a very good game last night.

Tuchel talks always about the value of players being in camp. 'The train is leaving the station,' is one of the England manager's more memorable quotes of recent times. Players like Cole Palmer, for example, have learned to their cost that missing meet-ups with injuries can be costly.

Bukayo Saka is not in that category and has plenty of credit in the bank with the England manager. However, Tuchel's fondness for Morgan Rogers is well known and Saka's absence does give him a way of getting the Chelsea player into his team. Rogers may be a number ten at heart but he was effective once again here out on the right side.

The 24-year-old was one of England's better players on a muted night against Croatia and he deserved his first half goal. He gives England a more direct, athletic dimension on the opposite flank to the more balletic offerings of Anthony Gordon. Food for thought for Tuchel at least as Saka continues his own battle against persistent injuries.

Bukayo Saka's long-term place in England's team could be under threat from Morgan Rogers

Newcastle United were pretty much an open door in the summer as they sold players left right and centre. Gordon to Barcelona to make sure the club was the right side of the financial guidelines and then Sandro Tonali to Tottenham and Bruno Guimaraes to Arsenal simply because the players made it known they wanted to go.

Strange, then, that Manchester United didn't make a proper move for left-back Lewis Hall. Admittedly this wasn't the most difficult match in which he will have ever played, but Hall was impressive once again.

With Luke Shaw so injury prone, Hall pretty much has the left-back berth sewn up for England but it feels as though he now needs to make the next step in his club career. United retain a nominal interest but who knows what incoming manager Mauricio Pochettino may think? It's hard to work out why United didn't try harder to sign him last summer. He has subsequently signed a new contract at Newcastle, of course.

#2616. Naz Reid landing spots: Four NBA contenders that make sense if Hornets look to move sharp-shooting big man

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

You could argue that before this season, there was not a single role player in the NBA more beloved by his own fanbase than Naz Reid. Simply uttering his name, devoid of context, became a popular meme among the Minnesota Timberwolves faithful in recent years, and for good reason. The former undrafted free agent grew into a Sixth Man of the Year winner and one of the best shooting bigs in basketball during his seven-year run with the Timberwolves. Leaving the only team he had ever known this offseason has proven difficult thus far.

Reid, 27, is posting big raw numbers in his first season as a full-time starter with the Charlotte Hornets, but there are bigger concerns under the surface. After shooting just under 57% on 2-pointers in Minnesota, he is at around 44% with the Hornets and struggling to score efficiently near the basket. His defense has raised eyebrows as well, and after he was benched in an early game against the Detroit Pistons, Hornets coach Charles Lee said that Reid "didn't meet our standards in the first half, and at halftime we made the decision that he wouldn't play in the second half."

Reid, along with an unprotected 2033 first-round pick, was one of the centerpieces of Charlotte's return in trading star guard LaMelo Ball to Minnesota. The 4-7 Hornets have struggled mightily without Ball, posting the NBA's worst offensive rating this season despite having the league's best offense from early December forward last season. Injuries have played a big part in those struggles, but at this stage, Reid's role as a foundational Hornets player moving forward is already coming into question. Timberwolves beat writer Jon Krawczynski of The Athletic even said on his podcast that the chances of Reid getting traded again are "very high."

"The Hornets now are clearly in a period of transition, and they decided that LaMelo Ball was not going to be a part of the team that they believe can eventually get to real contender status," Krawczynski explained. "They made a decision with that core group that they were not good enough as constructed and so they had to take a step back, amass some assets and go forward. And what that also means is that, A, the fans are going to be upset because they finally had a fun season last year and now it is going sideways again, but B, the possibilities of Naz Reid getting traded again are very high. This is a roster that I think is going to change over quite a bit over the next couple of years as the Hornets look for the right combination of people to really vault into what they hope is contention."

Krawczynski did not specify a timetable, and we've certainly seen frustrating starts turn into fruitful long-term partnerships, but all of this underlines just how difficult things have been for Reid and the Hornets so far this season. Charlotte knew what it was doing by trading Ball. The idea was to take a step back now to take a bigger step forward later. If that's still the idea here, there should be plenty of teams with real interest in Reid, so let's identify a few possible landing spots for the sweet-shooting big man.

The Warriors traded for and eventually re-signed Kristaps Porziņģis because they need big men who can shoot in a lineup featuring both Draymond Green and, presumably, Jimmy Butler eventually. Al Horford can cover some of those minutes, but he's 40 and can only be expected to play so much. Fortunately, Green's ability to defend across the positional spectrum means the Warriors don't necessarily need their center-sized shooter to actually defend centers. If he's big, he rebounds and he shoots, he'll fit.

This is Reid to a T. With Green on the team to actually guard the most dangerous centers and the combination of Butler and Yaxel Lendeborg providing size on the wing, the Warriors are fairly well-equipped to minimize Reid's weaknesses. His strengths are exactly what the Warriors need; the not-currently-getting-paid Porziņģis takes Golden State most of the way there when it comes to salary matching (with only a smaller salary like Gui Santos or De'Anthony Melton needed to close the hard cap gap), and the Warriors control almost all of their own future draft capital, so they have the ammunition they'd need to satisfy the Hornets.

The big question here -- especially with Stephen Curry now set to miss around a month with an oblique abdominal tear -- is how eager the Warriors are to invest in their present. Before the season, the answer should have been a resounding "not at all." But Curry was playing like an MVP candidate before he got hurt, and the emergence of Lendeborg as the Rookie of the Year favorite has arguably changed the equation. While the Warriors (8-4) may not be able to justify an all-in trade, giving up, say, one unprotected pick to nab the 27-year-old Reid, who can be a part of their post-Curry future as well as their present, might be a satisfactory compromise.

The Pistons have reportedly had an eye on Reid ever since his anticipated 2025 free agency, but he wound up re-signing with Minnesota before the opening bell even rang. The appeal is obvious. Two of Detroit's three best players, Ausar Thompson and Jalen Duren, are non-shooters. Having a big man who can shoot theoretically helps offset that deficit, particularly in lineups featuring just one of those two. Detroit tried that very strategy this offseason in acquiring John Collins. The results have been mixed, with the Pistons faring far better in the minutes Collins sits than the ones he plays. Reid is better and younger.

The Pistons are enormously flexible in how they could construct a deal. They control all of their own first-round picks, and they have a fair bit of breathing room beneath the luxury tax. That breathing room evaporates next season, though, when Thompson's rookie extension kicks in. This is where the decision calculus gets harder. Duren and Cade Cunningham are already making market rate. Thompson will be next season, and Duncan Robinson has simply proven too indispensable to move on from. Paying all four of those players plus Reid would leave precious little flexibility to add the second ball-handler Detroit badly needs.

Maybe the Pistons feel they're good enough as is to win without one, or they could be prepared to trade someone else out of their core down the line if they feel compelled to seek out that needed ball-handling addition. The Trajan Langdon-led front office is now in its third season at the helm, yet it has not traded a single first-round pick amid Detroit's ascent. The Pistons have been cautious with buy-now moves. Maybe Reid is the sort of player they'd splurge for, but considering how well the Pistons are playing, they will likely be cautious in shaking things up too much.

Cleveland's starting five simply hasn't worked this season. The Cavaliers are getting crushed with their five starters on the floor, and the Jarrett Allen-Evan Mobley duo, a frequent target of the rumor mill, is losing its minutes together by over five points per 100 possessions. That duo has never generated the elite rebounding that double-big lineups are supposed to create, and while they do a good job of defending shots at the rim, they give up so many of them that they net out as a fairly underwhelming rim defense. Peyton Watson is struggling to fit in as a small forward, but lineups featuring him and just one of Mobley or Allen are faring far better.

Swapping one of the bigs out for Reid, essentially trading defense for shooting, recalibrates the team in ways that theoretically create a friendlier environment for Watson. The Hornets, still presumably looking for a long-term starter at center, would likely have some degree of interest in either Mobley or Allen. The question is which makes more sense in a trade like this.

The answer is probably Allen. He's older. He's worse. He's more traditionally a center than Mobley, whom Cleveland has historically been reluctant to move up from power forward. But the on-off data is pretty clear this season: Cleveland is playing better with Allen on the floor than it is with Mobley. If the Cavaliers are going to go with a single big, it might behoove them to stick with the one they know can be a center. Mobley's 30% max contract is going to prove limiting down the line, especially with Donovan Mitchell starting a 35% supermax deal next season. Mobley would almost certainly net more in a trade than Allen would, and Charlotte has the pick surplus to make a pretty compelling offer if it wants to.

If Mobley is available in any way, shape or form by February, offers will come in from several teams. Not many have a package that makes more immediate sense than one built around Reid and Charlotte's picks, which Cleveland could either keep or redirect for other assets. If Cleveland and Charlotte do engage on Reid talks, though, Allen is the far likelier Cavaliers big man to become a Hornet.

We can't fully judge the Raptors until we see an extended stretch with a healthy Kawhi Leonard, but thus far, Toronto's shooting weakness elsewhere has been as severe as expected. The Raptors rank 24th in 3-point attempt rate and 27th in 3-point percentage as of this writing. Like Golden State, Toronto is perfectly equipped to cover for Reid's deficiencies as a rim protector. There isn't a better trio of defensive forwards in the NBA than Leonard, Scottie Barnes and Collin Murray-Boyles, and Murray-Boyles already plays a reasonable amount of center.

The money would presumably be RJ Barrett's expiring contract. Losing his shot-creation would sting, but with a healthy Leonard, they should be covered in that respect. The question is draft compensation. The Raptors already gave up unprotected picks in 2031 and 2033 for Leonard, leaving their 2029 selection as their only tradable, unencumbered pick. They could move their 2027 pick as well, though it has swap rights attached to the Oklahoma City Thunder, limiting its appeal. A swap or two would probably be needed here to seal the deal, but Toronto probably has the chips to pull this off if it's motivated enough.

Reid would eat up Toronto's room beneath the luxury tax line next season, but with all of their core players locked in, that shouldn't be much of an issue. The Raptors haven't started their tax clock yet, so a year or two above that line (and still well below the dreaded second apron) seems a small price to pay for a genuine championship contender.

#2615. Jacob Misiorowski named National League Cy Young winner: Brewers ace takes home unanimous honors

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Milwaukee Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski has unanimously been named National League Cy Young Award winner for the 2026 Major League Baseball season. He beat out the Phillies' Cristopher Sánchez and the Braves' Chris Sale.

Misiorowski takes home the honors of the Baseball Writers Association of America vote, which was revealed on Wednesday night. Misiorowski's triumph comes after a stellar age-24 season for the World Series champions:

In addition to the top-line numbers above, Misiorowski struck out 37.9% of opposing batters, which is tops in all of MLB and a sky-scraping figure for any pitcher, let alone a starter. Miz also paced the majors in FIP with a mark of 2.17, and his ERA+ of 232 is the 13th-highest figure by a qualifier ever in MLB. Misiorowski's WAR of 6.4 ranked third in the NL behind Sánchez and Jesús Luzardo of the Philadelphia Phillies.

Misiorowski was perhaps even more notable for his blazing fastball than he was the dominance of his statistical outputs. For the season, Misiorowski averaged 100.6 mph with his heavily used four-seamer, and on multiple occasions during 2026 he threw the fastest pitch on record, including this 105.5 mph offering from June:

105.5 MPH FROM JACOB MISIOROWSKI 🔥🔥 pic.twitter.com/wjvkdc7iWE

While Misiorowski's playoff performance was not part of the Cy Young criteria – ballots are submitted before the playoffs begin – he did post a 1.89 ERA in four starts this postseason for the Brewers, who wound up winning it all for the first time in franchise history.

Misiorowski is now the fourth Brewer to win the Cy Young Award. Corbin Burnes won in 2021, and Pete Vuckovich and Rollie Fingers won in 1982 and 1981, respectively, when the franchise was part of the American League.

Given his level of dominance and relative youth, Misiorowski figures to enter the 2027 season as the odds-on favorite to win the hardware again. If he does, he'll become the first back-to-back Cy Young winner in the NL since Jacob deGrom of the New York Mets in 2018 and 2019.

#2614. Caleb Wilson reportedly out 4-6 weeks with broken hand, taking away the only reason to watch the Bulls

The NBA injury train is showing no signs of slowing down as Bulls rookie Caleb Wilson will undergo surgery for a fractured right hand and miss four to six weeks of action, according to ESPN.

Wilson, the No. 4 pick in the 2026 NBA Draft, was injured in Wednesday night's loss to the Spurs. He was off to a great start for the otherwise struggling Bulls, who are now 1-9. He's an electric watch as a 6-foot-9, gliding athlete with every tool in the kit. He's averaging 18.9 points, 6.2 boards and nearly two steals a night so far. Before the injury, Wilson was listed at 15-1 to win Rookie of the Year, but within minutes of the news of his injury surfacing, those odds fell to 40-1 at FanDuel.

Before the injury, those were the fifth-best odds, which in most classes might not sound like a player having as good a start as Wilson, but this is an absolutely stacked rookie class with Yaxel Lendeborg being an actual All-Star candidate, Darius Acuff Jr. averaging over 26 points per game, Darryn Peterson averaging over 23 points in his last four and Cameron Boozer stuffing the stat sheet at 15.9 points, 9.8 rebounds and 5.5 assists a night for a Grizzlies team on the rise.

Wilson is the future in Chicago, and in the long term, that's all that matters. They almost have to look to trade Norman Powell before the deadline, and Nic Claxton should join him on the way out. Powell's deal is particularly priced to be moved as next year's $22.5 million is a team option. That's a good number for a player of Powell's worth but could also be an expiring deal for a team looking to use him for a championship push and then reassess over the summer with no long-term commitment.

However that plays out, the next month and change is going to be even more brutal for Bulls fans than the first three weeks of the season have been now that Wilson, like so many other of the league's most exciting players, is headed for street clothes.

This news of Wilson's injury comes on the same day that the Warriors listed Stephen Curry out for at least the next two weeks with an oblique tear. From Anthony Edwards to Jalen Williams, Tyrese Haliburton, Jaren Jackson Jr., Ja Morant, Kawhi Leonard, Cason Wallace, Paolo Banchero, Chet Holmgren, Jalen Duren, Curry and beyond, this is a massive issue that the NBA, in some capacity, needs to take meaningful steps toward at least attempting to resolve.

Fans are paying way too much money not to watch the best players, and for the Bulls, Wilson was the main attraction for a team that will struggle to win games. Outside of diehards who are going to tune in no matter what, absolutely no casual fan has an interest in watching Josh Giddey and Matas Buzelis on a 1-9 team. That's the harsh truth.

#2611. Cy Young winners Jacob Misiorowski and Cam Schlittler just put up a 2026 tandem not seen since 1905

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

To no one's real surprise, Jacob Misiorowski of the Milwaukee Brewers and Cam Schlittler of the New York Yankees have been named the 2026 Cy Young Award winners for, respectively, the National League and American League. Each was announced as the winner of Major League Baseball's topmost honor for pitchers, and each won the balloting in unanimous fashion. They are the first duo to win unanimously in the same year in their respective leagues since Justin Verlander and Sandy Alcantara in 2022 and just the third in MLB history.

Obviously, Cy Young winners have necessarily authored excellent seasons, but in the case of this year's winners, the descriptor "excellent" doesn't quite rise to meet the work of Misiorowski and Schlittler:

We could get into stuff, yes, as each has a blazing fastball that overwhelms hitters at the front end of a deep repertoire. This exercise, though, is more about how Misiorowski and Schlittler have overwhelmed the opposition when it comes to keeping runs off the board. You'll note all the strikeouts above, of course, but what may catch the eye is that each boasts a sub-2.00 ERA. That's a time-honored signifier of pitcher impeccability, even if ERA has its flaws.

To upgrade this familiar stat just a bit – and to put the two 2026 Cy Young winners' accomplishments into fitting context – we'll turn to ERA+. ERA+ is ERA adjusted to reflect league and home ballpark tendencies. An ERA+ of 100 represents the league average, and each point above or below that mark reflects a one-point change. For example, a pitcher with an ERA+ of 120 had a park- and league-adjusted ERA that was 20% better than the league average, while a pitcher with an ERA+ of 95 was 5% worse than the league average. So from the hurlers' standpoint, the higher the ERA+, the better.

This is all a necessary step when comparing pitchers across eras, because run–scoring environments have changed so drastically over the history of the sport. For example, Pedro Martinez's ERA of 1.74 in 2000, when teams were averaging more than five runs per game, means a lot more than, say, Charlie Chech's 1.74 ERA in 1908, when teams averaged 3.38 runs per game. That's where ERA+ comes in. Martinez in 2000 had an ERA+ of 291, or a park-adjusted ERA that was 191% (!) better than the league average. Chech in 1908 had the same ERA as Martinez in 2000, but his ERA+ of 136 was drastically worse.

As for the two moundsmen of present interest, Misiorowski this past season had an ERA+ of 232, which led the majors. Schlittler had an ERA+ of 215, which led the American League. Yes, they had those sub-2.00 ERAs, but, really, topping a 200 ERA+ is a much more impressive achievement. Counting Misiorowski and Schlittler but throwing out the pitchers who achieved the mark in the 60-game 2020 season (you should always throw out 2020), just 43 pitchers in MLB since 1900 have managed a 200 ERA+ or better across a qualifying number of innings. Over that same span and with 2020 also omitted, 201 pitchers have achieved a sub-2.00 ERA in a qualifying number of innings.

As you can imagine, it's a rarity to have not one but two pitchers in the same season who have a 200 ERA+ or better, as was the case this past season with Misiorowski and Schlittler. How rare? No season has ever given us more than two such qualifiers. Here's the full list of those across all of modern MLB history (i.e., since 1900):

Jacob Misiorowski, Brewers (232); Cam Schlittler, Yankees (215)

Jacob deGrom, Mets (218); Blake Snell, Rays (217)

Jake Arrieta, Cubs (215), Zack Greinke, Dodgers (222)

Roger Clemens, Blue Jays (222); Pedro Martinez, Expos (219)

Carl Lundgren, Cubs (211); Jack Pfiester, Cubs (214)

Christy Mathewson, Giants (233); Ed Reulbach, Cubs (209)

Yes, just six seasons have given us more than one 200 ERA+ pitcher, and this year's Miz-Cam combo marks just the third time that we've had one from each league. Accordingly, this marks just the third time that each Cy Young winner has reached the 200 ERA+ benchmark in a given season.

There's another, even more exclusive group that puts the Miz-Cam tandem in the proper context and hints at a future that's as bright as their present and their recent past. In 2026, Schlittler was in his age-25 campaign, while Misiorowski was in his age-24 season. So they're young as frontline aces go, and while you never want to make assumptions about pitcher health and durability in the current era, this duo's elite performance at both top-line and underlying level raises the possibility that each will win another Cy or two (or three) in the years to come.

Turning back to the 200 ERA+ defining stat, such youth in tandem with such excellence is all but unprecedented. Of the seasons listed just above, just 1905 featured two pitchers who, like Miz and Cam this past season, were age 25 or younger at the time. Mathewson, the inner-circle all-time great, was 24 that season and Reulbach was a 22-year-old rookie. We haven't seen something like that in more than 120 years.

Let's also note that Misiorowski and Shlittler, who each struck out more than 30% of opposing batters this season, absolutely have the stuff and foundational, forward-looking results to continue lording over their guild. Until that comes to pass, though, let's appreciate ther historical rare success and their even more historically rare combination of success and youth.

#2609. Rockets' Marcus Smart suspended three games for punching Warriors' Charles Bassey during in-game scuffle

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The NBA has suspended Houston Rockets guard Marcus Smart for three games for "throwing a punch that made contact with the face" of Golden State Warriors big man Charles Bassey, the league announced on Thursday.

The incident came late in the third quarter of Wednesday night's game in Houston. After Smart and Bassey got tangled up on the other end of the floor, Smart chased Bassey down and threw a punch at his head area. They were quickly broken up from there, and Smart was eventually ejected from the game with a flagrant-2 foul. Despite his absence, the Rockets went on to win the game, 115-108.

MARCUS SMART PUNCHES CHARLES BASSEY 😳 pic.twitter.com/MUsLlDHCz4

What triggered the incident? "I just talked to [Smart]. He said they got wrapped up, and [Smart]'s elbow that he hurt got bent up," Rockets coach Ime Udoka said after the game. "So, [Smart] said something to him. Bassey said, 'What are you going to do?' And he did it."

Bassey, on the other hand, blamed Smart for what happened. "He's been playing dirty the whole game," the Warriors big man said. "In the first half, I was trying to set a screen and he grabbed my knee. So I mean, he was playing dirty. [On the play in question], I think I was trying to get a rebound and he was grabbing my hand and I was trying to run back on defense. ... And then he got up on me and swung. Obviously that was weak. I think that was, honestly, fake toughness."

Charles Bassey on Marcus Smart throwing a punch at him: “Fake toughness.”“I don’t think he was trying to play. I think he was trying to get himself out of the game.” pic.twitter.com/ZxbgvUDeY9

As for what sort of words were exchanged between Smart and Bassey? "He said something to me," Bassey explained. "He said something like, 'Hey, don't do that.' I said, 'Do what?' It's a grown-man's league."

Smart is no stranger to NBA discipline. He has 12 ejections, nine fines (excluding flopping and technical foul fines) and two suspensions across his 13-year career. Now, the 9-3 Rockets will be without a key guard for the next three games, but fortunately for them, their next three opponents are all below .500: the Utah Jazz, Washington Wizards and Miami Heat.

#2606. LSU just dared the SEC to enforce its own rules. Now the conference has a major problem

So you say you want conference self-governance. College sports has gotten so out of control under the NCAA banner that the only path forward is to make the rules and enforce the rules, all on your own.

Welcome to the Thunderdome, SEC. When you walk inside, here you find LSU, once again playing by its own rules created by its own Louisiana judges, mocking you to your face and daring you to prove that you have the stomach to enforce rules the rest of the conference wants.

At the most fundamental level, what happened Wednesday night when the LSU men's basketball team put former NBA G League signee RJ Luis on the floor is the first big test of whether conference self-governance even has a chance of working now that the power leagues have tried and failed (thus far) to get the Protect College Sports Act to the finish line in Congress.

Barring a stunning reversal in the direction of the wind on Capitol Hill, the SEC and Big Ten have determined that this is the likely future of their enterprise in the near-term. In order to take back some control over eligibility rules from lawyers and judges, they have largely decided they must do it themselves.

Problem is, this requires good faith and cooperation among a lot of schools who mostly operate as independent entities and answer primarily to their fans and donors, not a conference office or some higher ethical standard about what's appropriate in college sports.

So all it takes is one bad-faith actor to mess everything up. And LSU is, more often than not, willing to push the envelope with Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry at the controls, a figurehead athletic director in Verge Ausberry and a head coach in Will Wade who thinks he's bulletproof after being fired from LSU in 2022 for major NCAA rules violations only to get the job back four years later.

LSU coach Will Wade laughs with greets Louisiana-Monroe coach Ryan Cross before the Tigers' win on Wednesday. (AP Photo/Ella Hall)

"It's like a scene from Dumb and Dumber," one longtime SEC administrator told Yahoo Sports.

The restrained and conservative way to frame the reaction when Luis checked in about eight minutes into LSU's 79-67 win over Louisiana-Monroe is that people across the SEC were furious and in some cases bewildered by the audacity of it all.

If you haven't followed this stuff closely enough to understand why, don't worry. It's complicated and mentally exhausting to keep up with every college eligibility mess that ends up in court these days.

But particularly with college basketball, some schools and coaches decided last season that they could add players who had left college years earlier and get them eligible through a temporary restraining order even if they had been drafted by NBA teams, signed two-way contracts or played in the G League. As you can imagine, the NCAA disagreed.

It also caused a major backlash, particularly within the SEC where former Alabama player Charles Bediako came back three years after turning pro, got a TRO, played five games and then became ineligible again after a different judge denied his request for a preliminary injunction.

In August, the SEC voted for new rules that would allow the conference to suspend coaches who bring back former pros and fine schools 50 percent of their athletic budgets, with commissioner Greg Sankey having wide latitude to impose more penalties. The motivation to pass this rule was — you guessed it — LSU football coach Lane Kiffin trying to bring back players who had left NFL training camps.

Ultimately, after a bunch of strongly worded statements and threats of expelling LSU from the league, LSU backed down and decided not to roster the former pros because they'd be crazy to do anything else. Right? Right?

Well, crazy is apparently back in town in the form of Wade, one of the sport's classic scoundrels (even he would most likely not mind that label) who cares little about his colleagues' affection and even less about, you know, rules. Remember, this is the same guy who was caught on an FBI wiretap detailing how he tried to buy a player before it was allowed, missed the 2019 NCAA tournament because he refused to cooperate with the school's ensuing investigation and then held onto his job three more years until the NCAA's allegations came finally down.

After firing Wade, LSU became really bad at basketball for four years. Empowered by Landry and the president he picked, Wade Rousse, LSU decided the only way to fix that was to bring back Wade, whose reputation had been cleansed by two years at McNeese State (where Rousse had been president previously) and one at NC State. With NCAA rules and judges across the country ushering in the pay-for-play era, Wade's past transgressions no longer mattered. What could go wrong?

Well, since LSU had no players when Wade returned, he unleashed his staff across the world to offer huge sums of money to a variety of players in Europe and former college players who would be willing to learn what the Louisiana legal system might be able to do for them. Enter Luis, who left St. John's in 2025 after being named Big East player of the year, went undrafted, signed a two-way contract with the Utah Jazz and even was part of a trade before his 2025-26 season was shut down due to injury.

LSU signed him, sparking multiple lawsuits in multiple places. The argument in favor of Luis is that, from a fairness standpoint, college basketball is filled with players from Europe who signed with club teams as young teenagers, technically making them just as professional. The argument against is that you have to draw the line somewhere, and if the college part of college basketball matters, you can't give eligibility to someone who willingly left college early to pursue a pro career and then wants to come back because things didn't quite work out.

Both perspectives have some validity. But in general, nearly everyone in college sports — and particularly within the SEC — supports the idea that adding G League players is ridiculous, even if there's a loophole or a TRO that allows it. Everyone except LSU.

This is where the self-governance concept meets the reality of what it will actually look like. By playing Luis — going two steps further than even Kiffin — a line in the sand has been drawn.

LSU is daring the SEC to go beyond strongly worded statements and do something drastic. Suspensions? Fines? A vote to expel them from the league? But then there's the legal implications, which are unclear and potentially unpredictable. In another win for billable hours, everyone is putting their general counsels to work.

The word early Thursday, prior to a meeting of SEC presidents, potentially centered on schools boycotting games against LSU. Particularly in states that aren't Louisiana, the thought is that this might hold up legally.

"I'm ready to take action," one league athletic director told Yahoo Sports. "But trying to cover all bases. These next 36 hours will be interesting."

Indeed, they will — with the concept of conference self-governance either proving to be a potential pathway toward college sports sanity or an idea that gets pronounced dead on arrival.

#2605. How can Warriors survive Stephen Curry's absence? Yaxel Lendeborg has to step up, but that's not all

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Golden State Warriors were riding high with an eight-game winning streak, a breakout rookie in Yaxel Lendeborg and Stephen Curry in MVP form heading into Wednesday's game vs. the Rockets. Then the record cut out at their party when Curry suffered an oblique tear that will cost him at least two weeks and maybe more.

If it is really just a two-week absence, he'll only miss six games and the Warriors will have dodged a bullet. But even that long without Curry is going to be an uphill battle for a team that, its hot start notwithstanding, already has little margin for error.

In general, there are obvious things that need to happen whenever a team loses the superstar that can cover for their mistakes: Limit turnovers (always a problem for the Warriors) and control the glass (Golden State is a relatively good rebounding team and should be able to be even better with some bigger non-Curry lineups; offensive boards go a long way for a team that is now likely to struggle to score for stretches). Winning the possession game will be vital.

You just have to be sharper in general without the ultimate bailout player on the floor. But more specifically, here are three things that probably need to happen for the Warriors to stay afloat without Curry.

After the Houston loss, Draymond Green had this to say about Lendeborg's 25-point, 10-rebound showing that helped fuel a post-Steph-injury surge and kept the Warriors in the game most of the way.

"The thing he's gonna have to learn to understand is, alright, Steph wasn't out there. [Durant] was off the court [for the Rockets]. You look around, you're probably the best player on the floor. Regardless of team. I think there was a point where he realized like, 'Oh, ding ding ding.' And he started attacking, and the game flipped for us.

"I think that's something he's going to have to realize really fast, is like, there will be often times where he could possibly be the best player on the floor regardless of the team. And we need him to show that, and he doesn't have a problem doing it."

This will never be truer than over these next couple of weeks. Lendeborg, a 24-year-old rookie, is now the Warriors' best player, and they need him to play like it. They need aggression. They need the production, from his iso scoring to creation for others to fueling and finishing as many transition attacks as possible.

He's capable of carrying a team. We saw it against the Clippers, when he went for 37 points and six assists with six 3-pointers and just one turnover as the go-to guy with Curry out.

But that was against one of the worst teams in the league (he gets Victor Wembanyama and the Spurs on Friday), and it was a one-night thing when maybe everyone wasn't quite aware of how good he really is. The secret is out now, and Lendeborg's name is going to be the one circled on every opponent's whiteboard moving forward. He'll get the overarching defensive focus. He'll get the double teams. And he'll have the burden of producing big numbers through all that.

There's no question that Lendeborg has looked incredible to start the year. He has the game and confidence to be a No. 1 option even just three weeks into his professional career. He's the Rookie of the Year favorite for a reason, and there has been justified talk about his being a real All-Star candidate. It's too early to be making statements like that, but for as long as Curry is out, Yaxel indeed needs to perform at that kind of level for an offense that doesn't really have anyone else capable of creating consistent advantages.

So far, the Warriors are making 16.5 3-pointers per game at a 39.7% clip. Both of those marks lead the league. A lot of this is Curry, who is making 4.3 triples per game at a truly absurd 45.7% rate given his shot difficulty, but it's not all him.

Give Brandin Podziemski the courtesy of rounding up three-tenths of a percent, and the Warriors have three guys currently making at least two 3s per game with at least a 40% conversion rate.

These are going to be the main gunners, but Golden State has other capable shooters. Georges Niang and Al Horford. LJ Cryer is about to see more time, and he's a 41.7% shooter. Will Richard is at 45.8%. These are all low-volume shooters who now have the green light.

This is how the Warriors stayed competitive against the Rockets: by jacking up 51 3s. They only made 17 of them, but that was still four more than the Rockets. That's a 12-point surplus, and the Warriors can still make plenty of mathematical hay with Curry out.

It won't be easy. His gravity creates a lot of these open looks guys enjoy, and that's where Lendeborg's ability to draw multiple defenders is going to be essential, but if everyone can combine to make just a few more 3s than normal, it can go a long way toward at least partially replacing Curry's 4.3 3s per game in the aggregate.

The Warriors are a top-10 defense (No. 9 if you remove garbage time, per Cleaning the Glass), and though they are giving up almost seven more points per 100 possessions with Curry off the floor, there's some deception in that stat.

Curry is a solid team defender and still better individually than a lot of people think, which is to say he's not going to be the reason your defense is bad. But he's also not the reason this Warriors defense is -- or at least has been -- good, and theoretically they should be just fine without him on that side of the ball. There's even a chance they get better.

De'Anthony Melton will likely start in his place. The Warriors, as mentioned, can play bigger. Curry's juice is infectious and that factors into defensive energy, and the upcoming schedule is a test (San Antonio, Boston and Memphis all register as top-eight offenses), but Green and company know the onus is on the defense to keep Golden State from taking on water without its captain. Are the Warriors up to the challenge?

#2604. Why a long-term mega deal for Tarik Skubal isn't actually all that risky

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The big prize of this free agent class is ace lefty and two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal. We've seen and will continue to see predictions that he's going to land a deal of around 8-10 years and topping $400 million. The knee-jerk reaction to such prognostications in many corners will be that he won't possibly be "worth" that much and that such a deal would be a huge "risk" to the signing team.

Let's stop right there. I don't think it's all that risky. There's risk for the team on every contract, especially pitchers, of course, but in Skubal, the signing team is getting a surefire ace for several years.

Let's examine some of the reasons why such an enormous deal isn't actually that dangerous.

Since returning from surgery in 2023, Skubal has been absurdly good. Across his ages 26-29 seasons, he's made 103 starts and has gone 50-20 with a 2.47 ERA (169 ERA+), 0.92 WHIP and 757 strikeouts in 626 ⅓ innings. He's only walked 109, or 1.6 per nine innings. He rarely gets hit hard, he rarely gives up many runs, he strikes out a high number of hitters and rarely walks any. Simply, he's been good at everything.

The recent track record here says this is the best pitcher in baseball, at least in the long view (we could argue Paul Skenes was better in 2025 and Jacob Misiorowski was better in 2026, to name two examples, but if we looked at 2023-present, it isn't all that close).

There isn't a dropoff in the postseason, either. In eight playoff starts, Skubal has a 2.13 ERA, 0.79 WHIP and 70 strikeouts against nine unintentional walks in 50 ⅔ innings.

Also, the career workload isn't anything to be concerned about. Skubal heads to his age-30 season now with only 925 ⅓ innings in the regular season. Even counting the playoffs doesn't get Skubal to 1,000 innings at the big-league level. Let's go back to Skenes. He's only 24 years old and already has 495 career innings. Another ace? Justin Verlander had 1,553 ⅔ career innings through his age-29 season.

There just isn't a ton of tread on these Skubal tires.

We'll hear plenty of consternation about Skubal being 30 years old next season as it relates to signing a long-term deal. We'll also hear people say a deal is risky due to his injury history. He had Tommy John surgery in college, flexor tendon surgery in 2022 and arthroscopic surgery (a new procedure using a Nanoscope) in 2026.

The simple matter is that pretty much every pitcher nowadays has had some sort of surgery on his arm, notably the elbow, and we've seen pitchers time and again bounce back after elbow surgery to perform at a high level.

Skubal just did it. He only missed roughly six weeks after his procedure this past season. He came back to make 19 starts after the surgery and posted a 2.73 ERA with 141 strikeouts in 115 ⅓ innings.

I mentioned Verlander above. Skubal is a multi-time Cy Young winner, so it's acceptable to look at some of the best pitchers in baseball and how they aged into their late-30s in recent memory.

Again, Skubal will be in his age-30 season in 2027. If he signs an eight-year deal, it'll run through his age-37 season.

For those so worried about the long-term finances of the team owner who ends up signing Skubal, are you sure you're really worried that he won't be productive through five, six, seven or even all eight years of that deal? Given his track record, talent, pitching arsenal, relatively low workload given his age and how well some of the best pitchers have fared through their mid-30s, he actually seems like a great bet.

A decade ago, the common talking point was that long and huge deals for pitchers never age well. That isn't actually the case, for the most part. Here are some of the biggest pitcher contracts of all time and how they unfolded (or are unfolding).

Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Dodgers, 12 years, $325 million -- He came over from Japan for his age-25 season, so this one was a different animal. Still, it sure doesn't seem like it'll be a bad deal, does it?

Gerrit Cole, Yankees, 9 years, $324 million -- Through six years of the deal, Cole has missed a chunk of time due to Tommy John surgery. He's also won a Cy Young, finished top four in Cy Young voting three times, been worth 22.4 WAR and was the ace of an American League pennant winner.

Stephen Strasburg, Nationals, 7 years, $245 million -- Here's the bust. Strasburg was never healthy again after the 2019 World Series title run. Still, the Nationals wouldn't have that title without him.

Justin Verlander, Tigers, 10 years, $219.5 million -- This was the deal that ran from 2010-19. During this deal, Verlander won two Cy Youngs (one in the second year of the deal, one in the final year), a World Series, three pennants, 160 games and led the league in pitcher WAR three times.

Max Fried, Yankees, 8 years, $218 million -- It's only been two years, but Fried is 24-10 with a 2.83 ERA and finished fourth in AL Cy Young voting in his first year.

David Price, Red Sox, 7 years, $217 million -- He won a World Series in the third year of the contract. Overall, he was 53-26 with a 3.78 ERA (118 ERA+) through the course of the deal.

Corbin Burnes, Diamondbacks, 6 years, $210 million -- Burnes had his first year of the deal interrupted by Tommy John surgery. He had a 2.66 ERA through 11 starts prior to the injury. The jury's still out, but he heads to his age-32 season fully recovered now.

Zack Greinke, 6 years, $206.5 million -- Over the course of this deal, Greinke was 77-39 with a 3.55 ERA (125 ERA+) and 19.9 WAR. He had a fourth-place Cy Young finish in there.

CC Sabathia, 9 years, $202 million -- The Yankees won the World Series in Sabathia's first year there and he started the deal with three straight top-four Cy Young finishes. Overall, during this deal, he was 120-73 with 27.1 WAR and had five straight 200-plus inning seasons.

Max Scherzer, 7 years, $191.4 million -- During this contract, Scherzer won two Cy Youngs, a World Series title and 99 games with a 2.75 ERA. He posted 41.8 WAR. In the seven years on this deal, Scherzer finished in the top five in Cy Young voting six times, with 2020 being the outlier.

We can close with this. Some people might not care for such a measure, particularly the salary cap crowd who will be worried about the owners paying too much. Regardless, let's stick with the general belief that each individual WAR (1.0 WAR) is worth a bit over $8 million per season.

By this measure, Skubal was worth $48.4 million in 2024, $53.7 million in 2025 and $41.7 million last season. Putting aside how much less money he actually made than what he was doing on the field, and knowing everything laid out above, I'll ask a simple question:

Are you sure a 10-year, $400 million deal for this guy would be a "risk?"

I think we could argue that it would be a bargain.
