#2602. NBA Washed Meter: Which late-30s (and older) stars still got it? And who's on the decline?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

We're in an age of outliers when it comes to aging superstars. Injuries are as persistent a problem in the NBA as they've ever been, yet the league is somehow also loaded with big names retaining relevance deep into their 30s (and in one notable case, beyond). Remember when the 2024 Olympics was supposed to be the swan song for LeBron James, Stephen Curry and Kevin Durant as the faces of the NBA? They're currently leading teams with a combined record of 27-10.

Some of the old guys very clearly still have it. Others are starting to slip. There are nine former All-NBA players in their age-36 season or later, so let's check in with each of them and measure how much they've had left in the tank thus far this season.

We're choosing to ignore injuries here, though they've obviously become a persistent issue for Curry. When he's been on the court, Curry has been closer to his peak than anyone on this list. Even after leaving Wednesday's loss to the Houston Rockets after five minutes, he's still averaging more than a point per minute. He has a higher effective field goal percentage than he did when he became the NBA's first unanimous MVP in 2016. He's even trimmed his turnover rate to a career-low. He's playing fewer minutes than he used to, but who cares when you're still getting MVP-caliber per-minute production out of him? Curry is our baseline. This is what it looks like for an old guy not to be washed.

He's playing fewer minutes than he once did, and he's getting the line less than he used to, but otherwise, you'd be hard-pressed to find a difference between this George and the version of him that last made an All-Star Team in 2024. If anything, he's been better this year, outscoring, outrebounding and outassisting his 2023-24 self on a per-minute basis. Only Dyson Daniels and Scottie Barnes are averaging more deflections per game among those who have played more than twice this season, and as a result, the Boston Celtics went from averaging the second-fewest turnovers per game in the NBA last season to the seventh-most thus far this season. Boston is getting everything it hoped for out of George this season.

He's taking the fewest shots of his career by far -- just 13.2 per game when he's never been below 16 -- but nobody in Houston is complaining. No Rocket is taking 16 shots per game, but five of them are at double-digit shot attempts and Houston has the No. 3 offense in the NBA. This egalitarian approach is working, especially with Alperen Sengun and Jabari Smith playing the best basketball of their careers and Fred VanVleet back in the fold to organize it all.

Still, you'd expect a volume decrease on a great team to lead to improved efficiency (not that there's ever been much room for improvement on that front for Durant), not a decline. Durant simply isn't shooting at his usual standards thus far. He's made up for it with a sharp uptick in free-throw rate (a new career high and it's not especially close), but that's going to be harder to maintain as the season progresses and we reach higher-leverage games. You shouldn't exactly be afraid for Kevin Durant's shooting, but coupled with his decrease in volume, he might be inching into a very slightly different phase of his career. He's still a star. He just may not quite be the NBA's apex shotmaker at 38.

The early returns -- especially in light of his torn Achilles -- have been tremendously positive. He's playing fewer minutes as so many of these players are, but he's scoring at roughly the per-minute rate he did during his two-year tenure with the Milwaukee Bucks. The raw 3-point numbers look worse than they are. We're still in tiny-sample territory, and Lillard shoots at such volume that only a few games could easily take him from the 33.3% figure he's at now up into the high-30s to which he's more accustomed. The eye test is there. Every few games he turns a quarter or two into Dame Time.

His 3-point attempt rate is a preposterous 62%. That's new for him, and welcome in a role meant to support Deni Avdija. He's never getting to the basket anymore, but that's what Avdija is around to do. Like Durant, he's getting to the line far more than one would expect for a player of his age. That likely won't sustain, especially with his drive numbers declining. Still, it'd be hard to ask for more out of a small guard returning from perhaps the most devastating injury in basketball. Box Plus-Minus rates him as a top-20 offensive player thus far this season, and while the other all-in-ones aren't quite as bullish, the overwhelming sentiment is that Portland is getting something relatively close to the standard Lillard experience at a fraction of the cost.

There are 133 players in the NBA averaging at least 26 minutes per game. Green is scoring less than half as many points per game (3.2) as any of them (Myles Turner, in 132nd, averages 6.7). The Warriors don't expect Green to score. They more or less never have. And it's not as though they truly play 4-on-5. Green remains heavily involved in the offense as a passing hub and hitting the offensive glass as much as ever. His defensive value remains through the roof. Even now, he's among the only players in the NBA that can credibly play center and guard -- not just switch, but truly guard -- on the perimeter.

But so much of what he does offensively is based on his tried-and-true two-man dance with Curry, who's now going to miss multiple weeks. Green has only played 28 minutes without Curry this season, but they've gone badly. We're about to find out how cumbersome a total non-scoring threat is to a basketball team that doesn't have the greatest shooter of all time. Green will still be valuable. But we're nearing the point where the offensive limitations he poses might become great enough to really make you wonder about his overall impact, especially with his defensive rebounding fading as well.

Look, your answer here is going to depend on how you're scaling this. When the bar is his legendary chase down block on Andre Iguodala, you'd be justified in watching James himself get chased down by two-way forward Jalen Slawson and saying "it doesn't matter how good he still he is, no player in the NBA has slipped as much as he has simply because of how high his starting point was." That just isn't the only consideration here. He's fallen from a lofty perch, but landed on his feet.

James has been declining gradually for years in subtle but noticeable ways. He drives less. He runs fewer pick and rolls and takes fewer shots out of isolations. Those numbers tick down bit-by-bit each year. He pads his point total with more transition buckets these days. He preserves his energy more carefully defensively, his value manifesting in his IQ and communication more than anything else. The Philadelphia 76ers are still getting plenty out of him. This roster full of ball-handlers needs a connector. James has always been capable of such a reduced role. He perfected it for the Los Angeles Lakers last season.

He's shooting badly from everywhere -- especially 3-point range, a quietly critical issue for Philadelphia considering Joel Embiid's decline on that front. The 76ers don't ask him for high usage, so getting the five or six hard drives he's capable of per night matter more than stacking the volume he once did. You'd rather have a few big plays than a bunch of lesser ones. How much of what we've seen this season is him pacing himself vs. the reality of playing a 24th NBA season won't really be knowable until bigger games come in the spring. For now, LeBron James is firmly a role player. He's a very valuable role player, one who does things, especially as a passer, that no other role player in NBA history has. But he's a role player nonetheless, and for someone as accomplished as James, that represents meaningful decline even if it doesn't constitute the end of the useful portion of his career.

The Miami Heat rank 23rd in 3-point percentage despite Thompson shooting above 40% on over nine attempts per game. That's how dire the offensive situation in Miami is. Andrew Wiggins and Tim Hardaway Jr. have struggled mightily so far. The entire theory of a team running most of its offense through bigs -- as Miami does with Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo -- rests on having high-level shooters to space the floor. Thompson is really the only trustworthy Heat shooter at this stage, and to his credit, he's holding up his end of the bargain on that front. He's never taken more 3s per minute than he is this year, and he's making plenty of them.

The trade-off here is that Thompson has been among the most vulnerable defensive players in the entire NBA this season, especially among those with real size. Thompson used to be an elite point-of-attack stopper. He transitioned into guarding bigger forwards as injuries and age sapped his mobility. Now, he's having trouble with just about everyone. Opponents are scoring 1.278 points per possession against him in isolation this season, per Synergy Sports. He really struggles to navigate screens at this stage. Late in games especially, Heat opponents are building a lot of their offense around finding and attacking Thompson.

The Heat are an average defense when Thompson sits and a terrible one when he plays. The former might be the problem here. The Heat were supposed to be great defensively with Antetokounmpo and Adebayo in the front court. They were supposed to be able to abide one defensive weak spot when the reality here is that almost everyone on the team has been worse on that end of the floor than Miami needed them to be. Thompson looks bad in part because everyone here does, but without the support we expected him to have, he's stuck out like a sore thumb defensively in ways that are going to prove problematic in the bigger games coming in April and May.

Harden has always been an extremely flawed player. You accepted the defensive issues and the turnovers and the slow, deliberate pace at which he played because he was such a uniquely gifted shot-creator that he remained enormously valuable in spite of those things. That isn't the case anymore. Not even close. Cleveland has been 19 points per 100 possessions better with Harden off the floor this season. As Danny Cunningham noted before their win over the New York Knicks Wednesday, every member of Cleveland's rotation had a worse net rating with Harden on the floor to that point in the season.

So much of Harden's game for the past two decades or so has started with the rim pressure he's generated. That's mostly been gone this season, and with it has been a lot of Harden's value as a passer. Less help means fewer corner 3s to pass into. When bigs aren't scared of him as a scorer, they don't frantically step up to meet him on drives, opening up his lethal lobs. Harden still gets to the line. He still self-creates plenty of 3s. But without that rim pressure, the flaws become less excusable.

Harden had his best game of the season on Wednesday, a 32-point outburst in that win over the Knicks. Maybe the first few weeks are a blip. Maybe he just wasn't in shape -- he's admitted he didn't play much pickup over the summer. But fitness has always been a concern, and at 37, it's possible and perhaps probable that he can't simply play his way back into shape during the season anymore. He looks like a different player, and if he is, whatever hopes Cleveland had of contending this season likely go up in smoke.

Harden and DeRozan are polar opposites as offensive players, but big picture, they're going through a similar process. You put up with DeRozan's antiquated shot-selection and poor defense because he got to the basket, got to the line and made all of his long 2s. Well, he's shooting 39% from mid-range this season, his lowest mark in more than a decade, and you can't live in mid-range on 39%. Now, DeRozan's decline as a finisher sticks out far more, and in turn, the fact that he can't really defend anymore becomes harder and harder to justify with minutes. Denver is getting crushed in all of DeRozan's minutes, with or without Nikola Jokić on the floor.

The Nuggets don't have much of a choice but to keep relying on DeRozan. This roster has a severe ball-handling deficit beyond Jokić and Jamal Murray. Someone else here needs to dribble, and DeRozan at least still manages to get to the line relatively often, and he does so without turning the ball. That's helpful. It's not enough. The entire premise of DeRozan as a valuable player rests on his ability to make shots most players shouldn't take. He isn't this season, and if that's the case, there are just few other ways he can make up for it to remain an impactful player.

#2601. MLB rumors: Phillies OF on the trading block, Blue Jays eye ex-Yankee, plus Mets, Mariners, Braves, Rays, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Thursday marks the final day of the General Manager meetings in Las Vegas. Though we haven't seen any major moves this offseason, we have seen an uptick in rumors in the past few days and that isn't a coincidence. Put a bunch of reporters and front-office execs in the same area for three or four days and chatter picks up, even if there isn't a ton of actual substance behind it.

Rumors are always fun, so let's round up the latest right here in addition to any news.

We have one of our first major-league deals of the offseason as the Braves have signed reliever Evan Phillips to a three-year, $35 million deal. Phillips ranked No. 34 on our top 50 free agent list.

Phillips, a 32-year-old right-hander, has been a setup man or closer for the Dodgers for the last several seasons. In returning from surgery last season, he appeared in 31 games, pitching to a 3.46 ERA and 1.07 WHIP with 33 strikeouts in 26 innings. The majority of his closing experience came in 2023 when he had 24 saves in 27 chances.

The Braves' closer last season was Raisel Iglesias, but he's a free agent. Holdover Robert Suarez could take over those duties while Phillips, lefty Dylan Lee and youngster Didier Fuentes are also in the late-inning mix.

The Blue Jays went from one of the best offensive teams in 2025 to one of the worst in 2026. They'd love a big bounceback from Vladimir Guerrero Jr., among other positive movements, but they also look for outside help. Might that help come in the form of free agent infielder Jazz Chisholm Jr.?

The Jays have met with representatives for Chisholm, reports Sportsnet.

Chisholm, 28, hit .231/.312/.399 last season, but had a huge 2025 and any signing team would be hoping for the 2025 version of Chisholm.

The Jays do have a capable incumbent second baseman in Ernie Clement, but either Clement or Chisholm can be used in the outfield and the Blue Jays certainly need outfield upgrades.

The Phillies have been telling opposing teams that they are not "locked into anything" regarding their current outfield situation, according to The Athletic, so much so that All-Star outfielder Brandon Marsh is available in a trade.

As things stand, with Bryce Harper moving back to first base, the Phillies would have Bryan De La Cruz in right, Justin Crawford in center and Marsh in left, but that all seems pretty fluid as they look to upgrade the ballclub and keep that window of contention open.

Marsh, 28, had a stellar start last season, leading to his first-ever All-Star Game. Through July 1, he hit .319/.352/.530. The rest of the way, however, he slashed .177/.241/.241, dragging him down overall to a 90 OPS+ and 0.4 WAR on the season.

The Mariners have shown interest in free agent left fielder Ian Happ, per MLB Network.

Happ, 32, has spent his entire 10-year MLB career with the Cubs, who drafted him in the first round all the way back in 2015. He was pretty consistent from 2022-25, averaging 3.9 WAR with a .251/.347/.433 (118 OPS+) line and winning four Gold Gloves. Last season, though, he dipped to .218/.326/.412 (103 OPS+) with 2.7 WAR. He still topped 20 home runs for the fifth time in the last six years.

The Mariners have a vacancy in left field with Randy Arozarena having hit free agency and a need to upgrade their offense.

Yesterday's big news was the Yankees' interest in free agent first/third baseman Alec Bohm and The Athletic reports that we can now add the Mets to the list of suitors.

Bohm hit .249/.315/.383 (87 OPS+) with 15 home runs, 88 RBI and -0.2 WAR last season. It might be surprising to see him garnering such interest on the open market, but there isn't much right-handed power out there and Bohm finished last season strong (.318/.402/.453 in his last 42 games). The Mets, meanwhile, are desperate for help at the cold corner after last year's disastrous Jorge Polanco experiment. Jared Young did provide a glimmer of hope at first base before suffering a concussion in September while colliding with a teammate on a play.

Free agent starting pitcher Dustin May has a decent market right now, according to MLB Network, with at least the Cubs, White Sox, Padres and Astros having shown interest in the right-hander.

May, 29, made 31 starts between the Cardinals and Brewers last season, going 7-9 with a 4.70 ERA in 145 ⅔ innings. He showed flashes of brilliance with the Cardinals and had a stretch from April 10 to June 15 during which he posted a 2.54 ERA in 12 starts, but in the end there was plenty of inconsistency and even bad, forcing him into a bullpen role in the playoffs for the champion Brewers.

Free agent catcher Ryan Jeffers has been extended the qualifying offer from the Twins, meaning he has to decide by net Tuesday whether to accept the one-year, $23.15 million contract or hit free agency. There's nothing that says a team can't re-sign a player after he declines their qualifying offer, of course, and it sounds like that path is possible in this case.

Jeffers will decline the QO and the Twins are interested in reaching a multi-year deal to bring him back, reports the Minnesota Star-Tribune. Jeffers hit .256/.353/.461 with 14 home runs for Minnesota in 2026, a standout line for a catcher, though he missed several months with a broken hamate. The Twins do have several catchers in their farm system, including Vahn Lackey, the No. 3 pick in last year's draft, and Eduardo Tait, who headlined the trade return for Jhoan Duran.

Much has been said and will continue to be said about the 2027 free agent class and how it looks relatively weak, especially on the position-player side, where the best players are the likes of Jazz Chisholm Jr., Seiya Suzuki, and the aforementioned Arozarena and Jeffers.

As we know, the Rays love to find avenues where they can exploit market inefficiencies. Their latest move might be to hit the trade market with center fielder Jonny DeLuca in anticipation of moving Victor Mesa Jr. to center, according to The Athletic.

DeLuca, 28, got more playing time than ever before in 2026, appearing in 112 games and getting 370 plate appearances. He hit .266/.300/.429 (101 OPS+) with 11 homers, 50 RBI, 17 steals and 1.7 WAR.

Fresh off a playoff berth despite the lowest payroll in all of baseball at a paltry $75ish million, the Guardians are planning to increase payroll. Or so they say.

"We'll go up," club president Chris Antonetti told The Athletic. "We have to."

The Guardians hosted six playoff games and made some money there, not to mention that they have a bunch of players hitting arbitration and surely they want to spend more to remain competitive. There's an added wrinkle here, too, which would be that the ownership side is really pushing hard for a salary cap when the upcoming CBA expires in a few weeks. With a cap comes a floor and we've seen MLB float proposals with salary floors in the $180 million range, or well more than double what the Guardians had last season.

So, yeah, I'd say the Guardians "have to" increase payroll, one way or another.

#2600. NBA Rookie of the Year race: Three players at top, but don't count out AJ Dybantsa, Darryn Peterson just yet

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

News broke on Thursday that Chicago Bulls forward Caleb Wilson will miss the next four to six weeks after fracturing his right hand. It marks the third separate hand injury Wilson has suffered during the last 11 months. He fractured his left hand and broke his right thumb during his freshman season at North Carolina, with the latter injury causing him to miss the end of the regular season.

Wilson was off to a hot start during his rookie season with the Bulls. The No. 4 overall pick was averaging 18.9 points, 6.2 rebounds and 1.8 steals in his first 10 games and was one of the few bright spots for the 1-9 Bulls.

Missing the next four to six weeks would keep Wilson out until at least mid to late December. Although there is no 65-game minimum requirement to win Rookie of the Year as with other NBA awards, missing an extended period of time will likely see Wilson fall behind in what should be one of the most competitive races in recent memory.

Entering Friday, there appears to be a clear-cut top five in this season's Rookie of the Year race. Warriors forward Yaxel Lendeborg, the No. 11 pick, is the current favorite (+115 at FanDuel). After Lendeborg, Grizzlies forward Cameron Boozer (+290) and Kings guard Darius Acuff Jr. (+320) have the shortest odds.

The top two picks in the draft -- Wizards forward AJ Dybantsa and Jazz guard Darryn Peterson -- are tied for fourth (+1600) in the odds. Wilson is next at +4000, with a steep drop-off after that.

Dybantsa missed the first four games of the season with an ankle sprain, while Peterson got off to a slower start than some of his peers but has looked fantastic for the shorthanded Jazz during the last week and a half.

The current odds for Rookie of the Year (as of Nov. 13) are below.

Less than a month into the NBA season, three players have separated themselves from the rest. Boozer opened the season as the favorite to win Rookie of the Year, with Wilson, Peterson and Dybantsa not far behind in the odds. However, two players outside of the top five picks in a loaded draft class are in position to crash the party. Here is a quick scouting report on what we have seen from Boozer, Acuff and Lendeborg and how they can continue to stay in the race.

The things Boozer did well in college have carried over to the NBA. Since the 2010-11 season, no player in college basketball had a better box plus/minus (18.75) than Boozer. His freshman season at Duke was better than those of Cooper Flagg and Zach Edey, both of whom also won national player of the year honors. It speaks to how Boozer can make an impact on the floor when he isn't scoring. He has a great feel for the game and is already one of the best outlet passers in the league. He crashes the boards hard and is physical on both ends of the floor.

However, one (small) concern was also an issue at times at Duke: rim finishing. Boozer struggled against bigger defenders at times in college, and he's running into the same thing in the NBA, shooting just 46.6% at the rim on 58 attempts, per Synergy. That number has improved over the last few games, but it's something Boozer will have to improve.

Lendeborg has been fantastic and is a major reason why the Warriors are off to an 8-4 start. The pressure will be even greater over the next several weeks while Stephen Curry is out with an injury. He routinely took advantage of mismatches at Michigan, and he's doing the same in the NBA. His all-around game has taken tremendous strides over the last 12 months and he's going to continue to get better.

Of course, the one knock on Lendeborg in the draft was age. He was the oldest player selected in the first round and just turned 24, but he's a perfect fit for Golden State given its win-now timeline. What has been most impressive for Lendeborg is his shooting. He is knocking down 42.6% of his 3-point attempts while taking 5.7 per game. Last season at Michigan, Dusty May told him to shoot more 3-pointers. It paid dividends for his overall game.

He is the most polarizing rookie in this class, and he is being asked to do more than his peers on a nightly basis. Since having a rough shooting night in his NBA debut against the Clippers, his efficiency has been much better. People who don't watch the Kings (how can you blame them?) might not realize that the box score doesn't tell the full story. Yes, Acuff has attempted over 20 shots per game in each of his first 11 games, but he is also 13th in the league in potential assists (12), 12th in assist points created, and 10th in total assists (80). The game is really slowing down for Acuff in a good way.

His passing was an underappreciated skill during his time at Arkansas. People will see the scoring numbers and immediately throw out a bad comparison for Acuff, but the truth is, Acuff is being asked to run the offense, be the primary scorer, and also facilitate. How many 19-year-olds in the NBA are being asked to do that? Right now, the answer is just him. Acuff will continue to put up numbers for a bad Kings team that is waiting for the trade deadline to deal some of the veterans on the roster.

ACUFF JR. JOINS LEBRON 👏In tonight's action, Darius Acuff Jr. (32 PTS, 10 AST) joined LeBron James (3x) as the only teenagers in NBA history to record 30+ points and 10+ assists in multiple games! pic.twitter.com/VmWshWmQZn

The debate surrounding the No. 1 pick was one of the biggest storylines in the lead-up to this year's draft. With Dybantsa going to Washington and Peterson to Utah, they ended up in similar situations on teams with established veterans that seemed ready to take the next step. But for the Jazz, it has been a nightmare season of injuries, with Jaren Jackson Jr. and Lauri Markkanen out for extended periods.

With everyone in the lineup, Peterson struggled to find a clear-cut role during his first few games. He finished in single digits in two of his first four games, which included taking just seven shots from the floor in his NBA debut. Coming out of high school, Peterson was best playing on-ball. However, when he got to Kansas, he played more off-ball. Part of that was due to cramping issues that sidelined him for an extended period, but Peterson has shown he can play both roles well.

darryn scored 26 tonight, a new career high #TakeNote presented by @ZionsBank pic.twitter.com/NaCyoa8kQv

The last four games have been excellent for Peterson and showed why he was the projected top pick entering last college basketball season. He has scored over 20 points in those last four, including a 26-point outburst against the Timberwolves. Peterson's shooting from beyond the arc has also been impressive during that stretch.

With so many key veterans out for Utah at the moment, Peterson has been pushed into an expanded role. It's going to be that way for the next several weeks. With Utah's season already looking like a mess, the organization's top priority should be developing Peterson into a primary option. If the last week is any indication, Peterson could get back into a very competitive Rookie of the Year race.

Thursday was a rough shooting night for Dybantsa during the most entertaining Wizards game of the entire season, which ended with a double-overtime loss at home to Detroit. Dybantsa shot just 2 of 10 and finished with five points -- the first time in his career he finished in single digits. However, Dybantsa did hit a clutch mid-range jumper to send the game to double overtime.

Outside of Kyshawn George taking seven shots in 26 minutes due to foul trouble, Dybantsa attempted the second-fewest (10) shots among starters. Dybantsa also didn't get to the free-throw line, which was shocking because one of his greatest strengths is drawing fouls.

Trae Young (23), Anthony Davis (21) and Alex Sarr (14) all attempted more shots against the Pistons. Dybantsa did contribute in other ways (eight rebounds and four assists), but that kind of game underlines why I'm hesitant to put Dybantsa in Tier 1 of the Rookie of the Year conversation. And trust me, it's not because of talent. Dybantsa is awesome.

AJ DYBANTSA FORCES 2OT!IN THE CLUTCH THE #1 PICK COMES THROUGH. pic.twitter.com/lsqG6bGNXX

The concern is that, with Davis and Young on the roster, the volume of shots for Dybantsa might not be there for him to win Rookie of the Year. Acuff is the primary option for the Kings. Lendeborg is now the de facto No. 1 option with Curry set to miss the next month. Peterson has been thrust into a larger role with veterans out. Boozer is putting up numbers on a nightly basis despite having a lower usage rate than Acuff, Wilson and Lendeborg.

Dybantsa is the face and future of Washington's franchise. He should be featured as such. If he isn't, he will likely fall behind the top three players in the race for the majority of the season.

Even outside of the top four names, several other rookies have performed well this season. Although they will likely be longshots to win Rookie of the Year, here are some sleepers and others worthy of recognition.

It's time for the Clippers to start Wagler. The impact he has on the game off the bench is impressive. If he is given more minutes, he will shine. The stat that stands out about Wagler is that he is shooting better from beyond the arc (35.4%) than inside the arc (29.7%). He is shooting 86% from the free-throw line, which is a positive indicator for future shooting success. He will be fine.

Mara was a player I thought could make an immediate impact as a rookie because of his defense and offensive efficiency. Mara is shooting 60.3% from the field and is blocking 1.8 shots per game. Check and check.

The flashes from Brown are must-see TV. It's the same sentiment as during his time at Louisville. If you put together a highlight tape of Brown's best plays, you would think he's the best guard in the class. He has played in just seven games this season and hasn't started because of a minutes restriction.

Flemings has been great in spots off the bench and even as a starter. He is one of the most efficient rookies in the class -- albeit on lower volume than his peers -- and is shooting 52.1% from the field, 42.9% from 3 and 72.7% from the charity stripe.

#2598. Astros slugger Yordan Alvarez named unanimous American League MVP after nearly winning 2026 Triple Crown

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Astros designated hitter Yordan Alvarez has won the 2026 American League MVP, the BBWAA announced Thursday night.

The Baseball Writers' Association of America ballot uses two voters from each of the 15 chapters housing AL teams. Each voter submits a ballot with 10 players, ranked 1-10. A first-place vote gets a player 14 points, while second place earns nine, third place eight, etc., until a 10th-place vote earns one point. Ballots are due before the playoffs begin, as this is a regular-season award.

Alvarez, 29, bounced back from an injury-riddled disaster in 2025, during which he only played in 48 games. This time around, he avoided the IL and appeared in 158 games. He hit .316/.432/.601 (190 OPS+) with 34 doubles, a triple, 42 home runs, 106 RBI, 105 runs and 6.8 WAR. He made a late run at the Triple Crown, missing out by one home run and seven RBI. He did lead the majors in all three triple slash categories, though, leading in average by five points, on-base percentage by a whopping 42 points -- he led the majors in walks -- and 31 points in slugging percentage. Add the latter two and his OPS victory was 90 points -- 1.033 to second place's .943 (National League MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong).

The only players in MLB history to lead the majors in all three triple slash categories:

Alvarez becomes just the third Astros player to win MVP after Jeff Bagwell in 1994 and Jose Altuve in 2017.

Rays third baseman Junior Caminero finished in second. At age 22, he played all 162 games, leading the Rays to the best AL record. He hit .276/.360/.524 (144 OPS+) with 42 home runs, 101 RBI and 100 runs, posting a 5.7 WAR. He's already made history, too, as the Rays had previously never had a player finish in the top five of MVP voting.

Royals shortstop Bobby Witt Jr. came in third. This is now his fourth straight season in the top seven and third straight season in the top four. He finished second in 2024. This season, he hit .281/.359/.441 (125 OPS+) with 33 doubles, 18 homers, 54 RBI, 94 runs, 45 steals and 6.7 WAR.

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong won the National League MVP award for the 2026 season unanimously, the BBWAA revealed Thursday evening.

The Baseball Writers' Association of America ballot uses two voters from each of the 15 chapters housing NL teams. Each voter submits a ballot with 10 players, ranked 1-10. A first-place vote gets a player 14 points, while second place earns nine, third place eight, etc., until a 10th-place vote earns one point. Ballots are due before the playoffs begin, as this is a regular-season award.

Though the results were unsurprising by the time the year wound down, going back to the start of the season, this marks a huge upset. Shohei Ohtani was the overwhelming favorite to win the award heading into the season and maintained favorite status through the All-Star break. A combination of his injuries and PCA's monster season turned the tide late.

Appearing in all 162 games, Crow-Armstrong hit .280/.372/.570 (156 OPS+) with 31 doubles, eight triples, 45 home runs, 107 RBI, 119 runs, 41 steals and 9.8 WAR. He led the majors in WAR, runs, home runs and total bases while leading the NL in slugging, OPS and OPS+. He became the seventh player in MLB history to join the 40-40 club (40 home runs and 40 steals in the same season). Further, he led the majors in multiple advanced defensive metrics, putting together one of the great all-around seasons from a position player in recent memory.

PCA joins the following list of Cubs to win MVP:

Ohtani, the four-time MVP, finishes in second. At the plate, Ohtani hit .275/.377/.512 with 26 doubles, four triples, 30 home runs, 81 RBI, 89 runs, 11 steals and 3.2 WAR. On the mound, he was 8-2 with a 1.79 ERA, 0.95 WHIP and 95 strikeouts in 85 ⅔ innings with 3.2 WAR.

The nationally underrated Brewers second baseman Brice Turang finishes in third. He still hasn't made an All-Star Game, though he did start 2026 as a member of Team USA in the World Baseball Classic. In the regular season, Turang hit .268/.366/.450 (124 OPS+) with 37 doubles, three triples, 21 home runs, 100 RBI, 102 runs and 7.3 WAR, rating out as one of the best defenders in baseball.

#2593. Now with an MVP, Pete Crow-Armstrong is on the path for an all-time great career. Where could he stack up?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The MVP winners were revealed Thursday evening and, unsurprisingly, the runaway unanimous winner in the National League was Pete Crow-Armstrong of the Cubs.

Crow-Armstrong had an all-time great regular season, which is what the annual Baseball Writers' Association of America award honors. He hit .280/.372/.570 with stellar defense, led the league in home runs (tied with Kyle Schwarber) and massively upgraded his on-base skills. Now, just a few months shy of his 25th birthday, he has an MVP to his name.

So what's next? To answer that, we'll look backwards.

Since integration, only eight center fielders have posted at least 8.0 WAR in a season age-25 or younger: Willie Mays, Mickey Mantle, Willie Davis, César Cedeño, Ken Griffey Jr., Andruw Jones, Mike Trout and PCA. The only ones to top PCA's 9.8 were Mays, Mantle and Trout. If we went back to pre-integration, Tris Speaker and Ty Cobb were the only others who bested PCA here.

Willie Davis was an inconsistent hitter through his age-23 season but had flashed a nice power-speed combo. Sound familiar? That gaudy 8.4 WAR total in 1964, though, was driven largely by monster defensive metrics. Davis hit .294/.316/.413 (110 OPS+) with 23 doubles, seven triples, 12 home runs, 77 RBI, 91 runs and 42 steals. There's little doubt that PCA's 2026 season dwarfed this one overall, and Davis was far behind Mays (11.0) for the league lead in WAR.

For the rest of his career, Davis averaged 3.1 WAR per season, and though he had good years, he never reached 6.0 WAR again. The WAR figure was, again, mostly driven by defense. He had several good offensive seasons, but his only 20-homer season came in 1962 when he was 22, two years prior to his career year.

Davis' career probably looks a lot like PCA's apparent upside before his home run barrage in the first half of 2025. He racked up over 60 career WAR with a decent batting average, excellent defense and excellent baserunning.

With PCA reaching 30-30 last year and 40-40 this year, though, the bar has been raised.

César Cedeño followed up his 8.0 WAR season with a 7.4 season at age 22 and 5.8 at age 23. He was very good through age 29 and, in fact, the most statistically similar player through both ages 27 and 28 was Hall of Famer Carl Yastrzemski. Things fell apart after that. As a quick and easy way to illustrate it, Cedeño amassed 49.4 WAR through his age-29 season and only 3.6 in his final six years.

It's easier to remember that Andruw Jones' career unfolded in similar fashion because we witnessed it not too long ago and then discussed his Hall of Fame candidacy during his nine turns on the ballot before he finally made it in. In Jones' 12 Braves' season, he racked up 368 home runs, 1,117 RBI and 61 WAR while generally being considered the best defensive center fielder in baseball. Once he left, in time for his age-31 season, Jones accrued just 1.7 WAR in his last five seasons.

Through Jones' age-28 season, the most statistically similar players are Bryce Harper and Frank Robinson.

To compare these two to Crow-Armstrong, the argument would be that he'll continue to look like one of the best players in baseball -- even if taking steps backward from being the very best in the 2026 regular season -- before falling apart once he's around 30 years old.

Certainly possible, but given the adjustments he's already not only been willing to make at the plate, but eager to make, I'm just not seeing him all of a sudden hitting a wall. Sure, at some point he'll start losing speed and that'll affect his defensive range and baserunning, but why would the plate skills deteriorate all of a sudden?

Then again, few saw it coming with Jones.

All three of these players were on the path to having an argument as the best player in history before injuries derailed them in their 30s and left them as mere "all-time greats."

Through Mickey Mantle's age-30 season, he had 90.7 WAR. He averaged 121 games per year in his final six seasons, putting up 19.5 WAR. Through  Ken Griffey Jr.'s age-30 season, he had 76.2 WAR. He played 10 more seasons, but only amassed 7.6 more WAR. Through Mike Trout's age-27 season, he had 72.1 WAR (his top statistical similars were Mantle, Robinson and Griffey). We'll skip 2020 for obvious reasons, but since then he's averaged 90 games and 3.0 WAR per season.

Even with the drop-offs, it would be surprising to see Crow-Armstrong reach this level because it's surprising to see any player reach this lofty standard. In career WAR among center fielders, Mantle is fourth, Trout is fifth and Griffey is sixth. They trail only Cobb, Speaker and the guy we're going to discuss next. Joe DiMaggio is seventh.

Despite the lofty standard PCA set for himself in 2026, coming close to Willie Mays' career would be jaw-droppingly shocking, and that is absolutely not intended as a slight.

Mays has an argument as the greatest player in baseball history and he put himself in that discussion by being good at everything and doing it all with great longevity. From his age-23 to -35 seasons, he led the majors in WAR eight times, leading the NL an additional two times. His worst seasons in that timeframe were 7.6 and 7.8 WAR. In that span, he also led the league in runs twice, hits once, triples three times, home runs three times, stolen bases four times, average once, on-base percentage once, slugging percentage five times and OPS five times.

Mays even posted 5.2 WAR at age 39 and 6.3 at age 40. He led the NL with a .425 OBP when he was 40 years old! He hit .345/.411/.667 at age 23.

Mays' 156.2 career WAR ranks third among position players all-time behind two guys you might have heard of: Barry Bonds (162.8) and Babe Ruth (162.3).

I feel pretty strongly Pete Crow-Armstrong isn't headed for a run at this career and that's just fine.

The realistic long-term range for the 2026 National League MVP seems somewhere between Cedeño and Mantle. It's a wide variance of outcomes between those two, obviously, as well it should be when the player we discuss is only 24 years old. For his name to be mentioned among these at all is a testament to the year Crow-Armstrong just put together.

#2592. Dejounte Murray landing spots: Three possible destinations after Pelicans guard requests trade

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

We have our first trade request of the 2026-27 NBA season. If you had Dejounte Murray on your bingo card, congratulations. The 2022 All-Star landed with the New Orleans Pelicans before the 2024-25 season, but his tenure there has been a mess and he requested a trade on Friday. He played 31 games in his first season, shooting worse than he ever had before tearing his Achilles. He returned late last season and played well, but the beginning of this season has been a mess.

Murray has remained in the starting lineup for the Pelicans, but New Orleans is 1-8 in the games he's played. They've lost his minutes by over 14 points per 100 possessions, he's shot poorly from basically everywhere on the floor, and he hasn't been a consistently impactful defender since he played for the San Antonio Spurs.

Meanwhile, Murray has made his displeasure public on several occasions.

At this stage, Murray's trade value is likely minimal. If a deal comes, it will likely involve a similarly bloated, multi-year contract attached to a player that a team is eager to move. Essentially, we're looking for "problem for problem" type of trades.

Three destinations make some degree of immediate sense.

The Suns are the first team to register known interest, according to Chris Haynes. Earlier this season, Haynes reported that the team's lack of a point guard had created frustration in the locker room. Phoenix started the season 1-5, but has since won four of its last five to somewhat right the ship.

Still, the Jalen Green experience has been a borderline disaster for Phoenix. The Suns have a staggering -15.7 net rating when Green plays and a +10.2 net rating when he sits. The former No. 2 overall pick was one of the primary pieces returned in the Kevin Durant trade, but his shooting has fallen off a cliff. He provides none of the playmaking that Devin Booker needs in a backcourt mate (which is part of why the Suns have fared so much better with Collin Gillespie on the floor in his place), and his defense is mostly nonexistent.

Both Murray and Green have player options for next season, with Green set to make $36 million and $30 million owed to Murray. The notoriously stingy Pelicans might insist on some form of compensation for taking on that extra money, but the premise here would essentially be the "problem for problem" structure we suggested above. With Murray gone, Jeremiah Fears could be the unquestioned starting point guard for the Pelicans. Green would either come off the bench or slot next to him at shooting guard, while Murray would be closer to the point guard archetype that Booker prefers.

It's by no means a perfect fit. Murray's weakness as a 3-point shooter would be problematic as the Suns have lost quite a bit of shooting since last season, and the Pelicans frankly have too many talented, shoot-first players as is. But it's at least an attempt at addressing real issues for both sides. The rebuilding Pelicans might at least like to take a look at a supremely gifted athlete, while the Suns would hope to get the point guard they feel they've lacked.

Andrew Wiggins has really struggled to fit into the new, Giannis Antetokounmpo-centric version of the Heat. The former No. 1 overall pick is averaging less than nine points per game on some of the worst shooting numbers of his career. His usually steady defense has slipped a fair bit on a unit that has been enormously disappointing as a whole, and, offensively, Miami's lack of a genuine shot-creating guard has proven problematic early in the season.

The Heat need a more reliable shot-generator than Murray, but after spending most of their assets on Antetokounmpo, their options are somewhat limited. This sort of swap would essentially be a bet that going from one of the NBA's worst organizations to one of its best could rejuvenate a former All-Star. Fitting a point guard that shoots poorly from deep on a Giannis team would be pretty problematic, but Miami would presumably stagger the two of them to limit their minutes together.

Such a swap would appeal to New Orleans for a few reasons. The first is contractual. Wiggins signed an unusual contract last offseason. He had a player option for the 2026-27 season, but rather than decline it and sign an entirely new deal, he picked it up and added a cheap two-year extension on the back end. He is making over $30 million this season but will dip to $16.3 million next season. That makes him an ideal trade target for a team that wants to save money. He can match salary with Murray in a trade now, but cost far less next year.

And then of course, there's the chance that Wiggins bounces back on a team that plays a bit more traditionally than Antetokounmpo-led teams can. Pelicans wings Trey Murphy III and Herbert Jones have been rumor mill fixtures for years, and with Saddiq Bey in place and a potentially rejuvenated Wiggins incoming, New Orleans would potentially feel a bit more comfortable cashing one of those other forwards out for draft picks since they'd have replacements in the building.

Murray is emphatically not the sort of player that the Hornets tend to target, especially at point guard. Charlotte wants to bomb 3-pointers. That is not now, nor has it ever been Murray's game. When Charlotte traded LaMelo Ball, it expected to be able to sustain a somewhat respectable offense with Coby White in his place and Kon Knueppel ascending. Well, Ball is starring in Minnesota and White and Knueppel have barely played.

The Hornets knew they were taking a step back this season with the Ball trade. They probably didn't expect the NBA's worst offensive rating, highest turnover rate and lowest true shooting percentage. Bringing in Murray could at least provide them with a stabilizing force at point guard, someone who could raise the floor enough to properly evaluate everyone else on the team moving forward.

The Hornets have a $40.8 million trade exception generated from moving Ball and almost $30 million in room below the tax line. They could nearly absorb Murray outright without sending out another contract, and they've shown a willingness to take on salary in exchange for draft capital. That would be the idea here.

The Hornets are not taking on Murray's player option for next season lightly. The Pelicans would have to make it worth their while with some form of first-round draft compensation. The Pelicans are probably hesitant to do so after all of the criticism they (justifiably) received for the Derik Queen trade, but Charlotte is probably the only team that can offer real financial relief for Murray at this point. If that's a priority, there might be a conversation here. If the Pelicans expect the Hornets to treat Murray as a real asset, the Hornets almost certainly pass.

#2591. Mauricio Pochettino is CONFIRMED as new Man United manager: Departing USA boss speaks out as he agrees to succeed Michael Carrick - but faces race against time for first game

Published: 07:02 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 07:51 EST, 13 November 2026

Manchester United have confirmed that Mauricio Pochettino has agreed to become their new head coach on a two-and-a-half-year contract at Old Trafford.

Pochettino will replace Michael Carrick who was sacked following 10 months in charge on Friday, after United agreed to pay more than £10million to buy him and his backroom staff out of their contracts with the US Soccer Federation.

The 54-year-old Argentine will take charge of the USA’s CONCACAF Nations League double-header against Haiti in Miami on Saturday and Cincinnati on Wednesday before beginning his new job as United boss on Wednesday. His first game will be against Liverpool at Anfield a week on Sunday.

There were no comments from Pochettino or United officials in Friday’s press release confirming his appointment because he remains contracted to US Soccer.

Pochettino said in the USMNT's statement: 'The opportunity to represent the USA crest was one of the greatest honors of my career. We are so grateful to the players for their commitment, to the fans for their belief, and to the Federation for always supporting our staff and creating the opportunities to impact the culture of soccer in this great country.'

Pochettino is due to give a pre-match press conference at 2.15pm on Friday, but is not expected to speak about United until he arrives next week.

United sources say that Pochettino’s experience, philosophy, personality and skill-set make him well suited for the job, as well as his record of developing individual talent and building excellent team cultures.

Mauricio Pochettino has been appointed as the Manchester United manager

Michael Carrick was sacked after the club made their worst start to the season in 40 years

A statement from the club read: ‘Mauricio Pochettino has agreed to become the Manchester United men’s head coach from 18 November.

‘The club has reached an agreement with the US Soccer Federation for Mauricio and his staff to be released after the conclusion of their responsibilities with the US men’s national team.

‘The Argentinian is renowned for his high-intensity, attacking style of football, his dedication to building strong, cohesive teams and his outstanding record of developing individual players.

‘Pochettino has consistently performed at the highest level of football across multiple leagues. He began his coaching career with Espanyol in 2009 before joining Southampton and achieving a club-record Premier League points tally in 2014.

‘During five full seasons at Tottenham Hotspur, Pochettino established the club as regular UEFA Champions League contenders, securing qualification in four consecutive seasons and leading the club to its first final in the competition in 2019.

‘In 2021, he joined Paris Saint-Germain, where he won the Ligue 1 title, the Coupe de France and the Trophée des Champions before joining Chelsea in 2023. Most recently he led the U.S. Men’s National Team to the Round of 16 at the FIFA World Cup.’

Earlier in the week, the club's chief executive Omar Berrada and Wilcox flew back from Monaco, where minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe ratified their decision to sack Carrick with the blessing of co-chairmen Joel and Avram Glazer.

Carrick arrived at United's training ground at 7.50am on Thursday morning and was dismissed.

He left at 10.18am, less than two and a half hours later. He became the first Premier League manager to be sacked this season.

United's statement read: 'After a disappointing start to the season, the club has come to the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions.

'Michael is, and always will be, a Manchester United legend. Just as he did as a player, he has conducted himself with the highest standards of dedication and professionalism throughout his time back with the club.

'His leadership and achievements last season will always be fondly remembered.'

Sources close to United say the club's leadership believe their squad of players is far better than the performances and results under Carrick indicated.

United feel that the squad are far better than their position in the Premier League shows

They gave the under-fire manager a chance to turn things around against Chelsea, Roma and Aston Villa but ultimately felt the team were not on the right path.

It has been a campaign in which United won just three matches, one of which came against Azerbaijani minnows FK Sabah, and they are yet to keep a clean sheet in the league.

Pochettino's United travel to Anfield on November 22 before a Champions League clash at Sporting Lisbon, Pochettino's first home game against Brentford and then away match at Newcastle.

#2590. MLB rumors: Rangers in mix for Sato, Dodgers seek infield help, Korean slugger could join free agent class

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The annual GM Meetings came and went this week with only one significant transaction: Evan Phillips signed with the Braves. Phillips, our 34th-ranked free agent, received a three-year deal worth $35 million. He'll replace Raisel Iglesias in Atlanta's bullpen and pair with Robert Suarez at the end of the game. The Braves could still re-sign Iglesias too, I suppose.

Otherwise, the GM Meetings brought a lot of rumors -- A LOT of rumors -- and presumably the groundwork was laid for moves that could be completed later this offseason. Here are our top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Friday's hot stove happenings.

The Rangers are among the teams with interest in Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato, reports The Athletic. Sato primarily played third base for the Hanshin Tigers, though he does not stand out defensively, and could land at first base or in the corner outfield in MLB. Texas could stand to upgrade at first base and could always slot Sato in at DH as well.

We ranked Sato as the fourth-best free agent available and the best free agent position player. The reigning Triple Crown winner in Japan hit .306/.383/.609 with 39 home runs in 2026. Sato, 28 in March, has some similarities to Munetaka Murakami as a lefty with big power and swing-and-miss concerns, though Sato is a much more aggressive hitter and won't walk as much as Murakami.

With Miguel Rojas retired, the Dodgers are looking to add a right-handed hitting infielder, according to The Athletic. Mookie Betts and Max Muncy are entrenched on the left side of the infield. Tommy Edman, a switch-hitter, is penciled in at second base, with fellow switch-hitter Alex Freeland next in line as depth. Freeland has not hit much in his limited MLB time, however.

This is not a great free agent class overall, but it does feature several utility infielders who hit right-handed. Among them are Mauricio Dubón, Ha-Seong Kim, Isiah Kiner-Falefa, and Edmundo Sosa. Glovemen Oswald Peraza (Angels) and Jared Triolo (Pirates) are potential trade targets. Rojas was a very productive role player for Los Angeles. He won't be so easy to replace.

The Padres are receiving calls about catchers Luis Campusano and Freddy Fermin, according to the San Diego Union-Tribune. Top prospect Ethan Salas was called up in September and became the youngest catcher to appear in the postseason in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series. Salas is the future behind the plate, making Campusano or Fermin (or perhaps both) expendable.

Campusano and Fermin are very different players. Campusano is a bat-first catcher who might be worth keeping given his age (28) and the fact that the Padres could slot him at DH. That said, those same qualities make him appealing to other teams. Fermin, 31, is a terrific defender who hasn't hit much the last few years. The Padres need pitching and could deal a catcher or two for an arm or two.

Samsung Lions outfielder Ja-Wook Koo has hired a new agent and is looking to make the jump to MLB, reports MLB.com. Koo, a 10-time All-Star and this year's Korean Series MVP, has been among the best hitters in the Korea Baseball Organization the last few years. The 33-year-old hit .371/.458/.581 with 15 homers and nearly as many walks (66) as strikeouts (71) in 2026.

Koo's age and the fact he's a left-handed hitter in a market inundated with left-handed hitting outfielders will work against him in free agency. He has a great track record in Korea, though, including a history of high contact rates, which could make him a cheaper and more appealing target than MLB free agents like Michael Conforto, Trent Grisham, Cedric Mullins, and Daulton Varsho.

#2589. Pressing Impossible: Amorim Loses to Hürzeler – MH

von Next Generation am 21.01.2025 in den Kategorien Premier League mit 0 Kommentaren

Rúben Amorim’s Manchester United faced Hürzeler’s Brighton on Matchday 22. While Manchester United focused on creating a pressing system that was as difficult as possible to bypass, Brighton once again showcased their incredibly challenging vertical play. You can find the tactical analysis of the match here.

Manchester United started in a nominal 3-2-4-1 formation, which transitioned into a classic 3-2-5 shape in possession and a 5-4-1 shape out of possession. Amorim initially placed particular emphasis on a pressing system that varied in height.

Meanwhile, Brighton began in a nominal 4-4-2 formation. In possession, Hürzeler’s trademark positional rotations, vertical runs, and decoy movements for effective vertical play were continuously on display. Accordingly, Brighton operated flexibly from a variety of shapes, such as 4-2-4, 3-1-4-2, 2-3-2-3, and more. This flexibility makes Brighton’s possession game almost impossible to define through formations alone.

Manchester United initially operated out of a 5-4-1 shape with varying defensive heights. This approach made it challenging for the opposition to play through, as different build-up phases required distinct patterns and connections. United’s central midfielders in the four-man line marked Brighton’s double pivot, Ayari and Baleba, man-to-man. The goal was to gain optimal control of Brighton’s central build-up play and apply immediate pressure whenever Brighton played through the middle.

However, Brighton controlled the game during the first 10 minutes. Their holding midfielders positioned themselves close to the backline, creating a large gap between Manchester United’s five-man defensive line and the four-man midfield. This space was then exploited with various runs. When facing high pressing, left-back Estupiñán moved asymmetrically into the left half-space behind United’s first pressing block. This movement utilized the moment when Amad stepped out to press one of Brighton’s center-backs after bypassing Zirkzee.

United failed to adjust their pressing to this build-up variation throughout the match. As a result, this same pattern played a key role in Brighton’s build-up to the goal that made it 1-3.

Against Manchester United’s mid-block, Brighton’s strikers, Welbeck and João Pedro, alternated their runs into the large space between the lines, targeting the gaps. This repeatedly allowed Brighton to bypass United’s first pressing line.

The 1-0 goal resulted from this setup, facilitated by a counter-movement. As striker Welbeck made a run into the space between the lines, he pulled his marker, De Ligt, a few steps out of the five-man backline. Simultaneously, winger Mitoma made a deep run into the space that opened up. De Ligt was caught in a dilemma between applying pressure and covering the depth. A long ball bypassed United’s entire pressing structure, leading to the goal.

Another reason for Brighton’s dominance in the first 10 minutes lay in their defensive work. United built up in a very positionally structured 3-2-4-1(/-5) shape. Brighton countered with a 4-4-2 in their high press and a 5-4-1 in their mid-block. With Minteh marking Diogo Dalot man-to-man on the flank, the two different defensive shapes emerged depending on Dalot’s positioning. Brighton’s two strikers also pressed United’s center-backs, Maguire and Yoro, on that side, applying intense pressure on the ball carriers on United’s left.

On the other side, winger Mitoma positioned himself centrally when De Ligt had possession, cutting off the passing lane to Amad, who was positioned in the half-space. If the ball was played to full-back Mazraoui, Mitoma shifted out from the center to press, creating a cover shadow into the center. This approach effectively prevented United from creating any significant attacking threat on that flank as well.

Around the 10th minute, the game shifted, and Brighton’s dominance began to fade. This was due to several adjustments made by United. To reduce the pressure on the ball carrier on the left side, the highly press-resistant Bruno Fernandes started to drop deeper, while the full-backs pushed higher. The resulting 3-3-4 shape was difficult for Brighton to press, as full-back Veltman, or the half-space defender in the five-man backline, was pulled out, and the space in behind could be exploited by either full-back Dalot or striker Zirkzee. This led to more possession phases for United and fewer pressing phases from Brighton.

Another adjustment United made came from their 5-4-1 mid-block. The half-space defenders, De Ligt and Yoro, became much more aggressive in stepping out from the five-man backline to defend against the strikers making runs into the large space between the lines. This prevented Brighton’s strikers from turning after bypassing the first pressing block. To defend long balls to Mitoma, Mazraoui prioritized covering the space behind the advancing De Ligt. As a result, Brighton struggled to exploit the space between the lines and couldn’t progress as effectively into depth from their own possession.

Additionally, Manchester United no longer pressed situationally from a 5-4-1 in a high press but instead switched to man-marking, with Zirkzee following the goalkeeper. This created much more pressure on the ball carriers for Brighton. Brighton also faced difficulties because the 5-4-1 system is much harder to break down than man-marking in a high press. This became evident in the sequence leading to the penalty goal. United suddenly switched to man-marking and forced the ball loss that preceded the penalty. United deservedly equalized.

After the 1-1, the game became more balanced. Brighton tried to break down the 5-4-1 mid-block, while United focused on their defensive game. When Manchester United switched to man-marking in the high press, Brighton continued to struggle and often lost possession. It is questionable why United didn’t press more boldly and high man-to-man during this phase to maintain better control of the game.

From Brighton’s perspective, a situational, more extreme overload at the moment of transition into high pressing—such as in the central space just behind the first pressing block—could have been a possible solution to challenge United’s man-marking, putting them in a dilemma between applying pressure and defending 1v1 on the wings.

In possession, Brighton’s players frequently adjusted their positioning with small movements, creating new passing lanes, changing passing angles, and occupying spaces that forced the opponent into pressing reactions. Below, I have outlined the main advantages of three of the most frequently used shapes by Brighton against United, as well as the necessary reactions from the opponent.

Another factor that makes Brighton’s vertical play difficult to defend is the continuous variety of space-creating or counter-movement runs into depth. These consistently create dilemmas and positional problems for the defenders. Below, I have graphically illustrated some selected runs used against United:

Despite Brighton’s possession game, Manchester United was able to prevent significant goal-scoring opportunities initially. From their 5-4-1 structure, the center-backs repeatedly defended aggressively, stepping out. Additionally, after bypassing the four-man midfield, it would drop back into position. This “recovery defense” made it difficult for Brighton to develop effective build-up play and exploit opened spaces. Furthermore, United’s players were well-prepared for potential through balls. In particular, the full-backs consistently intercepted balls played behind the defensive line.

Towards the end of the first half and into the second half, small (forced?) mistakes began to creep into United’s pressing. While the failure to step out with Ugarte in the man-marking high press in the 39th minute and the failure to step out with De Ligt in the space between the lines in the 38th minute went unpunished, the delayed step-out by Yoro led to Brighton’s deserved 1-2 at that point.

Especially in the second half, Brighton adapted to the man-marking high press by having center-backs step inside, breaking free from the cover shadow, when pressing the goalkeeper. This allowed them to find the open player in build-up, and Brighton lost possession less frequently.

Longer defensive phases in the mid-block for Manchester United followed. To break down this block, Brighton’s possession play became less positionally rigid. Much more frequently, certain zones were overloaded. In particular, the space between the lines and the half-spaces were repeatedly occupied by multiple players to create numerical superiority and apply pressure.

United, on the other hand, struggled to create any significant goal-scoring chances. The high press could have been more effective with a brief orientation from the player pressing the goalkeeper to position the inward-dropping center-back into a cover shadow. From the 5-4-1 mid-block, too few dangerous ball recoveries and transition situations were created.

Even from their own possession, Manchester United created too few goal-scoring opportunities. When Amorim’s team did get chances, it was typically through a ball played behind the wide players of the five-man backline. At the moment the press was triggered (when Brighton stepped out to the outer center-back), the forward half-space player dropped deep, and the winger made a run in behind. However, the lack of other ways to break the press led to too much predictability in United’s possession play.

As a result, the second half became more one-sided, with Brighton repeatedly pressing and trying to put United’s press under pressure. This ultimately succeeded, leading to a deserved 3-1 victory for Hürzeler’s team.

Amorim’s press, which was difficult to break down, was ultimately cracked by Hürzeler. It is questionable whether more frequent defensive pressing, alternating with situational man-marking high pressing, might have been a better approach against Brighton, in order to better tighten the space between the lines and the area behind the defense, making the game in depth more difficult. Despite a higher mid-block, Manchester United hardly created any dangerous transition situations. This is an area that needs improvement.

Hürzeler’s team, on the other hand, once again played highly attractive possession football. Frequent positional rotations, shifts in formations, overloads, and space-creating runs make Brighton’s possession game very enjoyable to watch. For the opponent, these constant shifts in zones over an extended period are incredibly difficult to defend. It is very likely that we will see more teams adopting similar principles in possession in the future.

Author: “MH” is a young analyst who regularly produces content for Spielverlagerung NextGen and TotalFootballAnalysis. On X, he can be found under Mh_sv5.

#2588. Cowboys make defensive coaching changes, name Mike Pettine as play caller as struggles continue

Three days after surrendering 584 yards — most ever in a home game — in a 46-40 loss to the 49ers, the Cowboys are making a big change in their defensive coaching responsibilities. Senior defensive analyst Mike Pettine will call defensive plays for Dallas, starting this weekend against the Titans, though first-year defensive coordinator Christian Parker will retain his job, CBS Sports' Garrett Podell has confirmed.

Sunday's performance was far from a one-off, as Dallas' defense ranks last in yards per game allowed (393.8), tied for last in points per game allowed (28.2) and 31st in yards per play allowed (6.2).

Against San Francisco, Dallas gave up three plays of 50+ yards — all for touchdowns. On the season, Dallas has allowed nine plays of 50+ yards, four more than any other team.

Monday, coach Brian Schottenheimer said the organization was "still in the process of going through all the film and evaluation" when asked about a change at defensive coordinator. Team owner Jerry Jones then hinted at a potential change Tuesday.

"We're talking about that, but I'm not going to talk about that here, but we are talking about those things," Jones said Tuesday on 105.3 The Fan in Dallas on Tuesday, via The Dallas Morning News.

Dallas is currently 4-6, with the defense largely to blame. The Cowboys' offense, in stark juxtaposition to the defense, ranks top 10 in yards per game, points per game and points per drive. After entering the season with high expectations, Dallas is fighting to simply stay in the playoff race, two games behind the Giants in the lowly NFC East.

The Cowboys initially brought Pettine, 60, aboard last month after Dallas' slow start on defense. He has not called plays since 2020, when he was the Packers' defensive coordinator. Green Bay finished ninth in total defense and 12th in scoring defense that year. Since then, he has bounced around, spending 2021 as a senior defensive assistant with the Bears and 2022-25 as a Vikings assistant head coach, working with outside linebackers in 2024 and 2025.

This is a considerable demotion — not in title, but certainly in responsibilities — for Parker, 34, who came to Dallas this season highly regarded after doing strong work as the Eagles' defensive backs and pass game coordinator from 2024-25.

Pettine has considerable history with both Schottenheimer and Parker. He spent 2009-11 as the Jets' defensive coordinator while Schottenheimer was New York's offensive coordinator. When he was with Green Bay, Pettine gave Parker his first NFL job as a defensive quality control coach.

One team that has "registered interest" in adding Murray is the Phoenix Suns, per Chris Haynes.

"Today, Dejounte Murray's representatives informed us of his request to be traded," the team said. "We will evaluate potential trade opportunities that are in the best interest of our organization."

ProPelsTalk, a Pelicans podcast, posted clips on social media highlighting purported mistakes Murray made during his team's fourth consecutive loss, to which Murray responded that fans have "no f--- ing clue what we are dealing with."

Let's hear it Mr social media coach, Gm and President? You have no f---ing clue what we dealing with. Murray finished with five points, four assists, and two rebounds in 28 minutes during the loss. This season, Murray is averaging 13.4 points, the lowest since his third season in the league with the San Antonio Spurs. On the same day Murray tweeted and then deleted that tweet, he also responded to another tweet, noting that the Pelicans are 1-8 with Murray and 3-0 without him.

#2586. Could Tarik Skubal take a short-term, high-AAV contract? Breaking down pros and cons

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The expectation is left-hander and two-time AL Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, far and away the best free agent available this offseason, will sign a record contract before the collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1. Barring a surprise agreement, the owners are almost certain to lock out the players at that time. Skubal is expected to sign before then.

Skubal, 30 later this month, is a Scott Boras client and Boras tends to shatter records, not beat them narrowly. There's a real chance Skubal signs a contract worth more than $400 million in the next two weeks or so. Excluding Shohei Ohtani, who is technically a pitcher but is really a two-way player, here are the largest pitching contracts in history:

Something like, say, eight years at $50 million a year would give Skubal a $400 million contract that obliterates the previous pitcher records for total guarantee and average annual value. Several big-market clubs are said to be pursuing Skubal (Blue Jays, Dodgers, Mets, etc.), who is a special free agent as an in-his-prime ace. Conditions are ripe for a record deal.

There is also a chance Skubal goes the Valdez route, or the Bo Bichette/Kyle Tucker route, and signs a short-term contract with a high annual salary. It might only be a small chance, but there is a chance. The Athletic reports the Dodgers prefer such an arrangement with Skubal. ESPN says Skubal has no interest in such a deal, though minds can always be changed.

With that in mind, here are the pros and cons of a high-dollar, short-term contract for Skubal. Keep in mind that such a contract is usually a three- or four-year deal with opt outs, not a straight one- or two-year contract, and Skubal wouldn't necessarily have to use the opt outs to re-enter free agency. He could leverage them into a new contract to stay with his team.

1. Maximize earnings. Plain and simple, a short-term contract would give Skubal a chance to max out his earnings by making free agency available to him again as soon as next offseason. Go out, have a typical Skubal season in 2027, and perhaps market forces push the demand even higher than it is right now. Remember that, along with a salary cap, there could be a salary floor in the future. Small-market contenders like, say, the Guardians or Rays could throw many millions at Skubal to reach the floor in the future.

2. Chance to set more records. This ties back to the last point. Skubal already set a new salary record for an arbitration-eligible player ($32 million in 2026) and he's positioned to set a new standard for pitcher contracts this offseason. Go back into free agency in a year or two, and Skubal (and Boras) could have a chance to break his own pitcher contract record. The record itself won't be a driving factor in that decision (the money will ultimately decide things), but it would be a nice feather in his cap.

3. Freedom to change teams. Sometimes things don't work out. I don't think Juan Soto expected to miss the postseason in the first two years of his record 15-year, $765 million contract with the Mets. It's entirely possible Skubal could find his next situation not to his liking for whatever reason. Maybe the team doesn't contend, maybe he clashes with the coaching staff, maybe he doesn't like the local breakfast taco options. There could be a million different reasons it doesn't work. A short-term, high-dollar deal would give Skubal an escape hatch and allow him to head elsewhere if things go sideways.

1. Injury and performance risk. All things considered, Skubal is a pretty safe bet on a long-term contract, though he is a pitcher, and pitchers get hurt. It's what they do. Skubal has had three elbow surgeries, including Tommy John surgery in 2017 and a minor procedure this May. If he gets hurt again, or his performance slips for whatever reason, then he could wind up costing himself in the big picture because he won't be able to opt out and sign a larger deal. A short-term, high-dollar contract will pay him handsomely. He won't struggle to put bread on the table. But injury/performance risk means Skubal could ultimately leave money on the table.

2. Potential salary cap. It is possible the next CBA will include a salary cap, which could limit Skubal's market and earning potential should he go back out into free agency in a year or two (or three). It's not just the cap itself either. MLB has proposed contract limits as part of the salary cap: five years at 15% of the cap for players who change teams, or six years at 16% of the cap for players who remain with their current team. Even if MLB doesn't get a salary cap and instead the competitive balance tax system remains in place with stiffer penalties, that could cost Skubal in the future. This offseason might be his last chance to sign in a truly free market.
